#### Vegetation

Pre-fire data. Detailed species lists of vascular plants existed for each site prior to the 1983 fire (White 1982). However, no quantitative data on pre-fire floristics or vegetation structure were available. Approximate pre-fire height was interpreted from pre-fire photographs and the height of burnt tips. Approximate pre-fire projective cover was also estimated from pre-fire field observations and photographs.

Data collection. Forty 1×3 m permanent quadrats (Table 1) surrounded by permanent extended plots (11×13 m) were used for data collection at 2, 6 and 10 months and in spring 1, 3, 7 and 10 years after fire. At site E, quadrats were in groups of three 20 m apart set at 90 m intervals along transect lines 300-350 m long. At subsite F1, quadrats were placed in a Maltese cross, and at subsite F2 they were distributed randomly.

Methods used to collect and analyse floristic and structural data (including canopy regrowth) and determine flowering and regeneration response have been previously described (Wark et al. 1987; Wark 1996).

Total species lists were made for each subsite at each survey, and these used to supplement quadrat data on floristics, flowering and regeneration strategies. As in Wark et al. 1987 and Wark 1996, the term 'total number of species' at a site (or subsite) refers to the total number of species recorded in the quadrats plus any additional species recorded at the site (or subsite). In the present paper, quadrat data alone are used to analyse the relationship between plant species richness and total vascular plant cover.

Girth of trunks of the overstorey and understorey were measured at 1.45 m (girth at breast height, GBH). Data on the eucalypt overstorey in open-forest was derived from measurements of a minimum of 20 trees of the tallest stratum. In this paper, the term understorey (or shrub stratum) will include the ground stratum; the term herb will be used to mean an herbaceous species; and the term graminoid will not be used.

Nomenclature of vascular plants follows Ross (1996); for Orchidaceae—Backhouse & Jeanes (1995); mosses—Scott & Stone (1976); liverworts—Scott (1985); and lichens—Filson & Rogers (1976). Introduced species were identified by the National Herbarium of Victoria.

The species described as Marchantia polymorpha in Wark et al. 1987 was incorrectly identified. It was in fact Marchantia berteroana Lehm. & Lindenb. (Scott 1985). Similarly, the fungus Omphalia chromacea is now known to be Gerronema postii (Fr.) Singer (May & Fuhrer 1989); and the herb Viola hederacea ssp. sieberiana now known to be Viola cleistogamoides. Name changes of vascular plants which have occurred since the first paper in this series (Wark et al. 1987) are given in Wark 1996 and in the Appendix of the present paper.

Regeneration strategies terminology follows Purdie (1977a, 1977b), namely: OSR=obligate seed regenerator (regenerating from seed or propagules only); FRR=facultative regrowth regenerator (regenerating by regrowth, and from seed or propagules); ORR=obligate regrowth regenerator (regenerating by regrowth only).

#### RESULTS
#### Regeneration strategies

(a) *Regeneration mechanisms and timing.* Regeneration was either by regrowth (from dormant buds, in stems, lignotubers, root tussocks, roots, rhizostolons, rhizomes, corms, tubers and tuberoids) from seed or propagules, or by both means (Table 5).

The first species to appear following the fire regenerated mainly by regrowth and included the ferns Cyathea australis, Pteridium esculentum and Todea barbara at three weeks, and sedges, rushes and other herbaceous species from four to five weeks. Regrowth of eucalypts commenced between two to three months. As mentioned earlier, the fire moss Funaria hygrometrica, the liverwort Marchantia berteroana, and fruiting bodies of the fungus Gerronema postii appeared 6-8 months after the fire, often forming extensive carpets on sheltered, damper slopes.

The three most conspicuous shrubs (Acacia verticillata, Goodenia ovata and Pultenaea daphnoides) germinated from seed between 2 and 6 months; and both north and south facing slopes in the ironbark forest looked like giant seed beds. By the end of year 1, all species capable of vegetative regrowth, and three-quarters of species which regenerated from seed, had appeared.

(b) *Regeneration strategies and life form groups.* Regeneration strategies and life form groups of all vascular species present 1-3 years post-fire and surviving till year 10 are shown in Table 6.

#### *Flowering response after fire*

(a) *Response during first spring.* Sixty per cent of species (94 of 157) which regenerated during year 1 flowered or produced spores (Table 5). Of these, 87 species were herbs. The rest included 2 ferns, 2 bryophytes, a fungus and 3 species of shrubs.

About 82% of all herbs recorded (including sedges, rushes, grasses, orchids, lilies, creepers and climbers) flowered in the first year after fire, and almost all the rest by year 2. Some ORR herbs, including autumn and winter-flowering orchids (Acianthus pusillus, Eriochilus cucullatus, Pterostylis parviflora), flowered from 5 months post-fire, as did Drosera whittakeri and Lagenifera gracilis.

There was conspicuous production of fruiting bodies by the moss Funaria hygrometrica, the liverwort Marchantia berteroana, and the fungus Gerronema postii from 6 months post-fire. By late spring, whole hillsides of the open-forest in damp areas (such as subsite E2) were coloured yellowish green by a carpet of fruiting bryophytes.

Grasses were conspicuous in the first spring after fire. Twenty-three species were identified at open-forest sites including 5 species of Danthonia (Table 3). Some species (eg. Danthonia induta and D. procera) flowered prolifically then were not seen in later years. Only 5 species of grasses were recorded in open-forest by year 10 (Table 3).

(b) *Orchid flowering response.* Nineteen species of terrestrial orchids appeared and flowered in 


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

REGENERATION IN THE ANGAHOOK-LORNE STATE PARK 31

open-forest during the first 3 years after fire. Though 16 species of orchids were recorded at subsite E1 during the 10 years, only 4 species appeared and flowered on this dry, eroded slope during year 1 (Table 3). Field observations suggest that the density of year 1 flowering of most species was higher than in pre-fire years.

Flowering of some orchid species was stimulated by fire. Two species (Caladenia menziesii and Prasophyllum odoratum), which appear but rarely flower in normal years, bloomed prolifically the spring after the fire. Seed-set accompanied post-fire flowering for all orchid species during years 1-3.

Only 3 species of orchids (Acianthus pusillus, Pterostylis nana, P. nutans) were recorded in the gully communities prior to the fire and in the 10 years post-fire. Field records made in similar communities near Moggs Creek prior to the fire, list 11 gully species (Acianthus caudatus, A. pusillus, Chiloglottis valida, Corybas dilatatus, C. incurvis, Cyrtostylis reniformis, Pterostylis curta, P. longifolia, P. nana, P. nutans, P. pedunculata— M. White; M. MacDonald, pers. comm.), all of which have been observed in the 10 years post-fire.

(c) *Flowering response of trees and shrubs.* Three shrubs (Goodenia ovata, Pimelea humilis, Lomatia ilicifolia) flowered in the first year. All other shrubs (92%) did not commence flowering till years 2 or 3, or later (Table 5). Lomatia ilicifolia (which is rarely seen to flower except after fire) flowered on new regrowth at 6-8 months. The juvenile phase of some shrubs (eg. Epacris impressa, G. ovata) was brief; flowering occurring within 2 years on plants only a few centimetres high.

By year 3, about two-thirds of the vascular plant species had flowered, including 4 species of trees (Eucalyptus baxteri, E. obliqua, E. tricarpa, E. willisii) and 27 species of shrubs. Not flowering at year 3 were 5 species of trees (Eucalyptus aromaphloia, E. cypellocarpa, E. globulus, E. ovata, E. viminalis), and 7 species of tall shrubs (Acacia dealbata, A. mearnsii, A. melanoxylon, Pomaderris aspera, P. ferruginea, Prostanthera lasianthos, Exocarpus cupressiformis). All 12 species flowered by 10 years post-fire.

By year 3, the percentage of OSR shrubs and OSR herbs flowering was 83% and 97% respectively and most of these species appeared to set seed. Little seed predation was observed either on plants or the soil.

(d) *Grazing during first 3 years.* No grazing of vegetation by native or introduced mammals was seen in the first 2.5 years after fire; though European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) were observed browsing herbs at subsite E1 late in year 3, and swamp wallabies (Wallabia bicolor) browsing shrubs at subsite E2 during years 7 and 10. Heavy grazing of young shrubs of Goodenia ovata by unidentified insect larvae occurred at all sites during years 1 and 2, with about 50% of the leaves being eaten. Extensive grazing of E. cypellocarpa coppice regrowth (by sawfly larvae, Perga sp.) was seen at subsite E2 during year 3.

#### DISCUSSION

This study has shown that, after a long fire-free interval, an E. tricarpa open-forest in the Anglesea-Aireys Inlet district was resilient to a single severe summer surface wildfire, supporting observations of Gill (1975, 1981) for dry sclerophyll forests in southern Australia.

The regeneration patterns of the open-forest community conform to the 'initial floristic composition' models of Egler (1954), and Purdie & Slatyer (1976), as 99% of vascular plant species present prior to fire re-established during the first three years.

The increase in the number of species of nonvascular plants in both open-forest and gully communities, with time, and as vascular plant cover increased, is similar to that recorded for the Anglesea heaths and heath woodlands (Wark 1996). The decrease in vascular plant species richness, as vascular plant projective cover increased, is similar to that described by Specht and Specht (1989) for sclerophyll communities in southern Australia, and was also observed in the heaths and heath woodlands of the Anglesea area (Wark 1996).

The failure of Amyema pendulum and Hymenophyllum cupressiforme to re-establish in the Ironbark forest and the gully communities respectively in the 10 years following the wildfire is not unexpected. All plants of A. pendulum were killed, and the mistletoe bird, Dicaeum hirundinacium (which is responsible for seed distribution and was uncommon in the Angahook-Lorne State Park before the fire—Conole & Baverstock 1984; Gill 1994), has not been seen in the area in the 10 years since 1983 (P. Reilly, pers. comm.; Reilly 1991). Filmy ferns such as H. cupressiforme, were rare in the district before the fire and probably have not re-established because the climate in the


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

32 MARGARET C. WARK

gully complexes has become drier. It may take many years for a cool microclimate suitable for these delicate plants to develop. Ashton & Frankenberg (1976) and Chesterfield et al. (1991) have commented that H. cupressiforme is badly affected by wildfire. No H. cupressiforme plants were seen 5 years after the 1983 wildfire in warm temperate rainforest in East Gippsland, Victoria (Chesterfield et al. 1991), and only a few plants 25 years after the 1951 wildfire in cool temperate rainforest at Lily Pilly Gully, Wilsons Promontory National Park, Victoria (D. H. Ashton, pers. comm.).

In the E. tricarpa dry sclerophyll forest, 60% of all species which regenerated following this wildfire were sprouters (FRS or ORR species). Similar high proportions of vegetative regenerators have been described for dry sclerophyll forests in Western Australia (Christensen & Kimber 1975), and the Australian Capital Territory (Purdie & Slatyer 1976). The high proportion (40%) of OSR regenerators seen probably reflects the intensity of the wildfire. It is known that in dry sclerophyll forests in Western Australia and New South Wales high intensity fires stimulate germination of hard-seeded understorey shrubs and fireweeds (Christensen & Kimber 1975; Christensen et al. 1981; Auld & O'Connell 1991). The dense shrub understoreys (dominated by Acacia and Pultenaea spp.) which established throughout most of the open-forest communities of the Anglesea-Aireys Inlet region following the Ash Wednesday wildfire, replaced the previously more open, often grassy, understorey (Parsons et al. 1977). Field records (Pat Denham, pers. comm.) suggest that the seed which germinated forming the shrub understorey in the E. tricarpa open-forest may have been stored in the soil for over 30 years—possibly longer if previous fires were of insufficient intensity to stimulate germination.

The slow rate of crown recovery of the E. tricarpa open-forest in the first three years after fire, may have been a result of both moisture stress, and low nutrient status. Leitch et al. (1983) showed increased hydrophobic properties of the soil at a forest site near Warburton, Victoria, where extensive sheet erosion (and resulting soil nutrient losses) occurred following the Ash Wednesday wildfires. They commented that similar sheet erosion also occurred in some of the Otway forests following the Ash Wednesday fires, and our data supports this.

Both moisture and nutrients released from ash are necessary for establishment of early post-fire bryophyte colonisers such as M. berteroana, F. hygrometrica and C. purpureus (G. A. M. Scott, pers. comm.; Cremer & Mount 1965; Southorn 1977), and stimulate post-fire flowering in orchids (Pate & Dixon 1982). The reduced incidence of the early post-fire bryophytes at subsite E1, and the failure of 75% of the orchid species at this site to flower in the first year after fire, suggest that both moisture and certain nutrients were lacking in these exposed sites. In 1983, Barnett (1984) noted a decrease in flowering of some orchid species following a surface fire in a Eucalyptus macrorhyncha open-forest, on a steep site with heavy clay soils at King Lake, Victoria, and suggested that one factor which may have affected flowering was the removal, by soil erosion, of fire-released nutrients. Changes in the soil microflora after the fire may also have been a factor. Similarly, the failure of the parasitic tall shrub E. cupressiformis to survive on these dry sites after its early re-establishment from seed and by regrowth, suggests also that insufficient moisture and nutrients may have been available to the young plants in the early years after fire.

The open-forest described in the present paper may not be totally resilient to frequent severe wildfires if burning occurs before the primary juvenile period of some OSR species. In the Ironbark forest, 3 species of OSR tall shrubs (Acacia mearnsii, A. dealbata, Pomaderris ferruginea) had neither flowered nor set seed 3 years after the fire. If another fire occurred before they reached reproductive maturity, they could be eliminated. Parsons et al. (1977) have commented that repeated burning at frequent intervals may convert an open-forest with a shrub understorey to an open-forest with a grassy understorey. Coaldrake (1961) has observed similar changes following sequential fires in the coastal lowlands of southern Queensland.

In the gully complexes (where peat fires did not occur) 52% of the species which regenerated following the wildfire were OSR species, regenerating from seed only. Similar high proportions (50-60%) of obligate seed regenerators have been described for wet sclerophyll forests in Western Australia (Christensen & Kimber 1975), Victoria and New South Wales (Ashton 1981). The regeneration patterns of the Anglesea gully communities (in the absence of peat fires) also conformed to the initial floristic composition models of Egler (1954) and Purdie and Slatyer (1976) as 99% of vascular plant species present prior to the fire re-established during the first 3 years.

#### *Flowering response after fire*

(a) *Response during first spring.* Sixty per cent of species (94 of 157) which regenerated during year 1 flowered or produced spores (Table 5). Of these, 87 species were herbs. The rest included 2 ferns, 2 bryophytes, a fungus and 3 species of shrubs.

About 82% of all herbs recorded (including sedges, rushes, grasses, orchids, lilies, creepers and climbers) flowered in the first year after fire, and almost all the rest by year 2. Some ORR herbs, including autumn and winter-flowering orchids (Acianthus pusillus, Eriochilus cucullatus, Pterostylis parviflora), flowered from 5 months post-fire, as did Drosera whittakeri and Lagenifera gracilis.

There was conspicuous production of fruiting bodies by the moss Funaria hygrometrica, the liverwort Marchantia berteroana, and the fungus Gerronema postii from 6 months post-fire. By late spring, whole hillsides of the open-forest in damp areas (such as subsite E2) were coloured yellowish green by a carpet of fruiting bryophytes.

Grasses were conspicuous in the first spring after fire. Twenty-three species were identified at open-forest sites including 5 species of Danthonia (Table 3). Some species (eg. Danthonia induta and D. procera) flowered prolifically then were not seen in later years. Only 5 species of grasses were recorded in open-forest by year 10 (Table 3).

(b) *Orchid flowering response.* Nineteen species of terrestrial orchids appeared and flowered in 


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

REGENERATION IN THE ANGAHOOK-LORNE STATE PARK 31

open-forest during the first 3 years after fire. Though 16 species of orchids were recorded at subsite E1 during the 10 years, only 4 species appeared and flowered on this dry, eroded slope during year 1 (Table 3). Field observations suggest that the density of year 1 flowering of most species was higher than in pre-fire years.

Flowering of some orchid species was stimulated by fire. Two species (Caladenia menziesii and Prasophyllum odoratum), which appear but rarely flower in normal years, bloomed prolifically the spring after the fire. Seed-set accompanied post-fire flowering for all orchid species during years 1-3.

Only 3 species of orchids (Acianthus pusillus, Pterostylis nana, P. nutans) were recorded in the gully communities prior to the fire and in the 10 years post-fire. Field records made in similar communities near Moggs Creek prior to the fire, list 11 gully species (Acianthus caudatus, A. pusillus, Chiloglottis valida, Corybas dilatatus, C. incurvis, Cyrtostylis reniformis, Pterostylis curta, P. longifolia, P. nana, P. nutans, P. pedunculata— M. White; M. MacDonald, pers. comm.), all of which have been observed in the 10 years post-fire.

(c) *Flowering response of trees and shrubs.* Three shrubs (Goodenia ovata, Pimelea humilis, Lomatia ilicifolia) flowered in the first year. All other shrubs (92%) did not commence flowering till years 2 or 3, or later (Table 5). Lomatia ilicifolia (which is rarely seen to flower except after fire) flowered on new regrowth at 6-8 months. The juvenile phase of some shrubs (eg. Epacris impressa, G. ovata) was brief; flowering occurring within 2 years on plants only a few centimetres high.

By year 3, about two-thirds of the vascular plant species had flowered, including 4 species of trees (Eucalyptus baxteri, E. obliqua, E. tricarpa, E. willisii) and 27 species of shrubs. Not flowering at year 3 were 5 species of trees (Eucalyptus aromaphloia, E. cypellocarpa, E. globulus, E. ovata, E. viminalis), and 7 species of tall shrubs (Acacia dealbata, A. mearnsii, A. melanoxylon, Pomaderris aspera, P. ferruginea, Prostanthera lasianthos, Exocarpus cupressiformis). All 12 species flowered by 10 years post-fire.

By year 3, the percentage of OSR shrubs and OSR herbs flowering was 83% and 97% respectively and most of these species appeared to set seed. Little seed predation was observed either on plants or the soil.

(d) *Grazing during first 3 years.* No grazing of vegetation by native or introduced mammals was seen in the first 2.5 years after fire; though European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) were observed browsing herbs at subsite E1 late in year 3, and swamp wallabies (Wallabia bicolor) browsing shrubs at subsite E2 during years 7 and 10. Heavy grazing of young shrubs of Goodenia ovata by unidentified insect larvae occurred at all sites during years 1 and 2, with about 50% of the leaves being eaten. Extensive grazing of E. cypellocarpa coppice regrowth (by sawfly larvae, Perga sp.) was seen at subsite E2 during year 3.

#### DISCUSSION

This study has shown that, after a long fire-free interval, an E. tricarpa open-forest in the Anglesea-Aireys Inlet district was resilient to a single severe summer surface wildfire, supporting observations of Gill (1975, 1981) for dry sclerophyll forests in southern Australia.

The regeneration patterns of the open-forest community conform to the 'initial floristic composition' models of Egler (1954), and Purdie & Slatyer (1976), as 99% of vascular plant species present prior to fire re-established during the first three years.

The increase in the number of species of nonvascular plants in both open-forest and gully communities, with time, and as vascular plant cover increased, is similar to that recorded for the Anglesea heaths and heath woodlands (Wark 1996). The decrease in vascular plant species richness, as vascular plant projective cover increased, is similar to that described by Specht and Specht (1989) for sclerophyll communities in southern Australia, and was also observed in the heaths and heath woodlands of the Anglesea area (Wark 1996).

The failure of Amyema pendulum and Hymenophyllum cupressiforme to re-establish in the Ironbark forest and the gully communities respectively in the 10 years following the wildfire is not unexpected. All plants of A. pendulum were killed, and the mistletoe bird, Dicaeum hirundinacium (which is responsible for seed distribution and was uncommon in the Angahook-Lorne State Park before the fire—Conole & Baverstock 1984; Gill 1994), has not been seen in the area in the 10 years since 1983 (P. Reilly, pers. comm.; Reilly 1991). Filmy ferns such as H. cupressiforme, were rare in the district before the fire and probably have not re-established because the climate in the


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

32 MARGARET C. WARK

gully complexes has become drier. It may take many years for a cool microclimate suitable for these delicate plants to develop. Ashton & Frankenberg (1976) and Chesterfield et al. (1991) have commented that H. cupressiforme is badly affected by wildfire. No H. cupressiforme plants were seen 5 years after the 1983 wildfire in warm temperate rainforest in East Gippsland, Victoria (Chesterfield et al. 1991), and only a few plants 25 years after the 1951 wildfire in cool temperate rainforest at Lily Pilly Gully, Wilsons Promontory National Park, Victoria (D. H. Ashton, pers. comm.).

In the E. tricarpa dry sclerophyll forest, 60% of all species which regenerated following this wildfire were sprouters (FRS or ORR species). Similar high proportions of vegetative regenerators have been described for dry sclerophyll forests in Western Australia (Christensen & Kimber 1975), and the Australian Capital Territory (Purdie & Slatyer 1976). The high proportion (40%) of OSR regenerators seen probably reflects the intensity of the wildfire. It is known that in dry sclerophyll forests in Western Australia and New South Wales high intensity fires stimulate germination of hard-seeded understorey shrubs and fireweeds (Christensen & Kimber 1975; Christensen et al. 1981; Auld & O'Connell 1991). The dense shrub understoreys (dominated by Acacia and Pultenaea spp.) which established throughout most of the open-forest communities of the Anglesea-Aireys Inlet region following the Ash Wednesday wildfire, replaced the previously more open, often grassy, understorey (Parsons et al. 1977). Field records (Pat Denham, pers. comm.) suggest that the seed which germinated forming the shrub understorey in the E. tricarpa open-forest may have been stored in the soil for over 30 years—possibly longer if previous fires were of insufficient intensity to stimulate germination.

The slow rate of crown recovery of the E. tricarpa open-forest in the first three years after fire, may have been a result of both moisture stress, and low nutrient status. Leitch et al. (1983) showed increased hydrophobic properties of the soil at a forest site near Warburton, Victoria, where extensive sheet erosion (and resulting soil nutrient losses) occurred following the Ash Wednesday wildfires. They commented that similar sheet erosion also occurred in some of the Otway forests following the Ash Wednesday fires, and our data supports this.

Both moisture and nutrients released from ash are necessary for establishment of early post-fire bryophyte colonisers such as M. berteroana, F. hygrometrica and C. purpureus (G. A. M. Scott, pers. comm.; Cremer & Mount 1965; Southorn 1977), and stimulate post-fire flowering in orchids (Pate & Dixon 1982). The reduced incidence of the early post-fire bryophytes at subsite E1, and the failure of 75% of the orchid species at this site to flower in the first year after fire, suggest that both moisture and certain nutrients were lacking in these exposed sites. In 1983, Barnett (1984) noted a decrease in flowering of some orchid species following a surface fire in a Eucalyptus macrorhyncha open-forest, on a steep site with heavy clay soils at King Lake, Victoria, and suggested that one factor which may have affected flowering was the removal, by soil erosion, of fire-released nutrients. Changes in the soil microflora after the fire may also have been a factor. Similarly, the failure of the parasitic tall shrub E. cupressiformis to survive on these dry sites after its early re-establishment from seed and by regrowth, suggests also that insufficient moisture and nutrients may have been available to the young plants in the early years after fire.

The open-forest described in the present paper may not be totally resilient to frequent severe wildfires if burning occurs before the primary juvenile period of some OSR species. In the Ironbark forest, 3 species of OSR tall shrubs (Acacia mearnsii, A. dealbata, Pomaderris ferruginea) had neither flowered nor set seed 3 years after the fire. If another fire occurred before they reached reproductive maturity, they could be eliminated. Parsons et al. (1977) have commented that repeated burning at frequent intervals may convert an open-forest with a shrub understorey to an open-forest with a grassy understorey. Coaldrake (1961) has observed similar changes following sequential fires in the coastal lowlands of southern Queensland.

In the gully complexes (where peat fires did not occur) 52% of the species which regenerated following the wildfire were OSR species, regenerating from seed only. Similar high proportions (50-60%) of obligate seed regenerators have been described for wet sclerophyll forests in Western Australia (Christensen & Kimber 1975), Victoria and New South Wales (Ashton 1981). The regeneration patterns of the Anglesea gully communities (in the absence of peat fires) also conformed to the initial floristic composition models of Egler (1954) and Purdie and Slatyer (1976) as 99% of vascular plant species present prior to the fire re-established during the first 3 years.

23:{1}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
25:## **Flowering, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling recruitment in two pyrogenic flowering resprouters**
39:#### **Introduction**
45:{2}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
55:#### **Methods**
57:#### *Study species*
63:#### *Sites*
69:#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*
73:#### *Estimates of seed production and seedling establishment*
77:{3}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

89:#### *Seed predation*
103:#### *Seedling dispersal*
111:#### *Analyses*
117:{4}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
135:#### **Results**
137:#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*
139:For both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, the first flowering after the January 1994 fires occurred in late winter (August) of 1995, some 19 months after the January 1994 fire. This pattern was found at all study sites and more generally across Royal National Park. Fruits matured in the following autumn (March–June 1996), with *D*. *excelsa* first releasing seeds in March 1996 and *T*. *speciosissima* in April 1996. Consequently, seeds were not released into the post-fire habitat until some 25–26 months after the passage of the January 1994 fire. Seed fall was quite prolonged with some seeds still in fruits in June (both species). *D. excelsa* plants in the study plots did not flower in any of the subsequent 5 years, while most *T*. *speciosissima* individuals flowered again the following year and a few in three of the subsequent 4 years (Table 1), with a similar timing of flowering and fruiting to that observed in 1995–1996.
141:#### *Fruit and seed production*
143:In *D*. *excelsa*, the number, and hence density, of flowering plants varied considerably between plots within sites, ranging from six at Site 1, plot 1 (0.2 m–2) to 39 at Site 2, plot 2 (1.3 m–2) (Table 1). There were no significant differences between sites in the mean numbers of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.86, *P* = 0.45) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 9.94, *P* = 0.09) produced per fruiting plant, although there were almost twice as many follicles produced at Site 1, plot 1, than at Site 2, plot 2 (Table 1). For *T*. *speciosissima*, the total number of individuals that flowered between 1995 and 2000 varied from 14 at Site 1 to 24 at Site 3 (Table 1). There was no significant difference in the mean number of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.4, *P* = 0.59) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 0.003, *P* = 0.96) per fruiting plant between sites across the 1995–1997 flowering seasons. *D. excelsa* had greater seed production per follicle than *T*. *speciosissima* (104, 105 *v.* 11 seeds per follicle, respectively, Table 2). There were no significant differences in the number of seeds per follicle between sites for *T*. *speciosissima* (*F*1,46 = 0.43, *P* = 0.52) or *D*. *excelsa* (*F*1,42 = 0.08, *P* = 0.93) (Table 2). The estimated density of seeds produced by *D*. *excelsa* varied greatly, although not significantly (*F*1,2 = 4.76, *P* = 0.16) across sites, with Site 1 producing 9.9 (±0.4 s.e.) seeds per m<sup>2</sup> and Site 2 producing 17.7 (±3.6 s.e.) (Table 3). The lack of significance in this comparison is likely to be a result of the considerable variation between plots at Site 2, with one plot producing approximately 1.5 times as many seeds as the other. This in turn was largely because of the much higher density of flowering and fruiting plants in plot 2 than in plot 1 of Site 2 (Table 1). There were no significant differences in seed density of *T*. *speciosissima* between sites (*F*1,2 = 1.11, *P* = 0.40) or among years (*F*2,2 = 4.19, *P* = 0.19). In the first post-fire fruiting year (1996), the estimated density of seeds
145:{5}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
147:produced was 1.1 seeds per m<sup>2</sup> at both sites (Table 3). Seed production was higher in the second fruiting year at Site 2, but lower at Site 1. Despite the lack of significance of a year effect in the analysis, at both sites seed production declined dramatically by the third fruiting year (1997) and no seeds were produced in subsequent years (Table 1). Total post-fire seed production by *D*. *excelsa* was considerably greater than by *T*. *speciosissima* (e.g. 9.9 *v*. 2.0 seeds per m<sup>2</sup> , 2350 *v*. 430 seeds per flowering plant for *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, respectively, at Site 1) (Table 3).
149:#### *Seed dispersal*
153:#### *Seed predation*
157:**Table 1. Estimates of reproductive output in** *Doryanthes excelsa* **and** *Telopea speciosissima* Data for infructescences and follicles are means per fruiting adult (standard errors are given in parentheses). There was no flowering in the 1994 flowering season for either study species
163:**Table 2. Estimates of the number of seeds per follicle in**  *Doryanthes excelsa* **and** *Telopea speciosissima* Data are means ± standard errors
167:**Table 3. The estimated density of seeds released by** *Doryanthes excelsa* **and** *Telopea speciosissima***, the density of seedlings in spring 1998 and the proportion of seeds (%) that had established as seedlings by spring 1998 (4.5 years post-fire)**
173:{6}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
183:{7}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
193:**Table 4. Analysis of the spatial distributions of seeds and seedlings for** *Doryanthes excelsa* **and** *Telopea speciosissima*
197:{8}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
203:## *Seedling establishment*
205:The first seed germination event after the 1994 fire for both species was observed in June 1996, some 2.5 years after the fire. Seedlings were found at all sites. The density of seedlings that had established and persisted up to 1998 for *D*. *excelsa* varied from 0.28 (± 0.08) per m2 at Site 2 to 0.31 (± 0.15) per m2 at Site 1 (Table 3). There were no significant differences in seedling densities between sites (*F*1,16 = 0.02, *P* = 0.88) or plots within sites (*F*1,16 = 0.47, *P* = 0.63). For *T*. *speciosissima*, the density of seedlings established by 1998, from any one post-fire seed-crop, ranged from 0 per m2 at Site 3 following 1998 fruiting to 0.15 per m2 ± 0.07 at Site 1 following 1997 fruiting, although fruiting year did not significantly (*F*2,2 = 1.44, *P* = 0.41) influence seedling establishment (Table 3). For all fruiting seasons combined, there were approximately 10 times as many seedlings
211:{9}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
213:recruited at Site 1 than at Site 3 in *T*. *speciosissima* (*F*1,24 = 11.1, *P* = 0.003, Table 3).
215:The percentage of the seeds released that established as seedlings varied between species, sites and years. For *D*. *excelsa*, both sites had low establishment percentages (1.6–3.1%) (Table 3). For *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, the percentage seedling establishment was low (0–1.9%), but comparable to *D*. *excelsa*, while at Site 1 percentage seedling establishment was higher (11.2–20.6%) (Table 3). The resultant seedling densities per m<sup>2</sup> were similar for both species, except for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, where they were an order of magnitude lower (Table 3). For *T*. *speciosissima*, these seedling densities reflected an accumulation of cohorts of seedlings from 3 years of postfire fruiting, compared with 1 year for *D*. *excelsa*. In terms of seedlings per flowering plant there was more variation, with results for *D*. *excelsa* ranging from 64.5 seedlings per flowering adult at Site 1, plot 1 to 6 at Site 2, plot 2. For *T*. *speciosissima* for the three fruiting seasons combined, the range was from 22.7 seedlings per flowering adult at Site 1 to 0.1 at Site 3.
217:## *Seedling distribution*
219:The distribution of seedlings around adults differed significantly from that of seeds (Table 4). In all cases, a greater proportion of seedlings occurred further from the adult than suggested by the seed distributions. When the distribution of seeds was compared with that of seedlings around isolated individuals of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, there was a difference in the shape of the respective distributions, with the distribution of seedlings fairly uniform up to about 7 m from an adult (Fig. 4). In contrast to the distribution of seeds (Fig. 1*a*), there was not a large proportion of seedlings near adults. These data suggest that seedlings had a similar likelihood of occurring anywhere up to 7 m from their parent. Where there were overlapping seed shadows from parent plants in *D*. *excelsa*, the distribution of seedlings (Fig. 5*a*) was uneven, but more or less uniform in density up to 4 m from a parent plant, with a decline further away. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the overall shape of the distributions of seeds and seedlings was similar, despite the significant difference in the distributions. The greatest proportion of seedlings occurred further from the adult than for seeds and the tail extended further from the adult (Figs 1*b*, 5*b*). The maximum difference in distributions tended to occur within 2 m from adults, suggesting that there is some interaction between adults and seedling recruitment that leads to reduced recruitment less than 2 m from adults. This effect appeared to be most pronounced in *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1. In both species, recruits were located well beyond the limit of seeds detected in the seed-distribution surveys, suggesting either occasional long-distance dispersal directly from the infructescence or later (i.e. after our survey) dispersal occurring at ground level (Harper 1977; Hammill *et al.* 1998).
221:#### **Discussion**
225:**Table 5. Summary of literature giving time to recruitment of seedlings after fire for species of different seed bank types from various fire-prone environments**
231:{10}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
235:Both species took some 2.5 years after the fire to establish seedlings. Other species either cohabiting with *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, or from other fire-prone habitats, established seedlings much sooner. In general, those species with a soil seed bank mostly establish seedlings within the first year after a fire, while those with a canopy seed bank mostly release seed in the first 6 months (Lamont and Barker 1988; Lamont *et al.* 1991) and establish seedlings in the first year (Table 5). Even other species that rely on post-fire flowering for seedling establishment appear to be 0.5–1.5 years quicker than *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* in establishing seedlings post-fire (Table 5). Among other Australian species, Auld (1986) found that for the shrub *Angophora hispida*, establishment occurred within about 18 months, while seedlings of shrubby *Xanthorrhoea* spp. were observed 18 months to 2 years after fire (Benwell 1998; Curtis 1998; Taylor *et al.* 1998). This is also the case in other fire-prone areas of the world, including Californian sage scrub, Florida sand pine scrub and South African fynbos (Table 5). By the time seedlings of *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* are becoming established, much of the space, light and nutrients made available by the fire may have been captured by other species (both resprouting plants and seedlings). This will be particularly the case for seedlings from the second and third fruit crops post-fire in *T*. *speciosissima*. In other vegetation types, resprouting species may be able to continue recruiting new seedlings several years after fire (e.g. *Garberia heterophylla* in Florida, Abrahamson and Abrahamson 1996). Curtis (1998) observed seedlings of the arborescent monocot, *X*. *australis*, at sites unburnt for about 100 years. However, such inter-fire recruitment has rarely been observed in the post-fire environment of *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*. Thus, despite the tolerance of their adults to fire, the persistence of these species may in part be due to their large seed size, which ensures that seedlings have sufficient reserves to
243:{11}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
245:and subsequently eat seeds. Differences in seed losses between study species at Site 1 for low-density seeds may reflect a difference in palatability of seeds or degree of predator satiation, given the much greater seed production in *D*. *excelsa* (Table 1). At Site 3 for *T*. *speciosissima*, losses were high for seeds at high and low densities. While predator satiation may occur in the immediate post-fire period when species with canopy seed banks release seeds, it appears that such effects are less important by the time *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* release seeds. Consequently, if recruitment is not limited by a lack of safe sites, then seed losses to predators are likely to have had an impact on the magnitude of seedling recruitment, particularly for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3.
247:Seedling recruitment was observed at all sites, but generally only a small percentage of the seeds released successfully established (≤4%, Table 3). The exception was at Site 1 for *T*. *speciosissima* where about 14% of all seeds released post-fire were established as seedlings. However, seedling densities by 1998 were comparable between *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1 (0.3 per m<sup>2</sup> , Table 3), resulting from the much greater seed production of *D*. *excelsa* at this site (Table 1). In contrast, for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, seedling densities were an order of magnitude lower (0.03 per m<sup>2</sup> , Table 3), even though there was no significant difference in seed production to *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1.

These species rely on post-fire flowering and the production of non-dormant seeds to exploit favourable post-fire establishment and growth conditions. For two such pyrogenic flowering species (*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa and *Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br.), we examined the timing of seed release, patterns of fruit production, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling establishment following a fire in the Sydney region of southeastern Australia. Both species took some 19 months after the fire to flower and the first seeds were released 2 years after the fire. *D*. *excelsa* flowered and fruited only once after the fire. For *T*. *speciosissima*, plants also flowered at least once more in the subsequent 5 years, but produced seed in only the first three post-fire flowering years. Fruit production differed between species, with fruiting individuals of *D*. *excelsa* producing fewer infructescences, similar numbers of follicles, but many more seeds per follicle than fruiting individuals of *T*. *speciosissima*. Ultimately, *D*. *excelsa* produced approximately six times as many seeds per m2 and four times as many seeds per adult in one flowering season than *T*. *speciosissima* did after four flowering (three successful fruiting) seasons. Seeds were passively dispersed from fruits borne 3–4 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 1–2 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) above the ground. Most seeds were found within 5 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 3 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) of parent plants. The primary seed shadow of both species was a poor predictor of the distribution of seedlings, with more seedlings occurring further from the adults than expected from the distribution of seeds. Seed loss to predators was high in both species in exclusion experiments where mammals had access to clumps of seeds (77–88%). It was variable and generally lower (8–65%) in experiments where seeds were not locally clumped. However, for *T*. *speciosissima*, at one site, some 65% of seeds were lost to mammals and invertebrates in these latter experiments. At this site, these losses appeared to influence subsequent recruitment levels, as very low seedling densities were observed. For both species, germination of seedlings first occurred some 2.5–3 years after the passage of the fire. The percentage of seeds produced to seedlings successfully established was low in *D*. *excelsa* (2–3%) and more variable across sites and years in *T*. *speciosissima* (0–18%). Resultant post-fire seedling densities of *D*. *excelsa* (two sites) and *T*. *speciosissima* at one site were similar, but they were much lower at the *T*. *speciosissima* site that had high levels of seed predation. Both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* are amongst the slowest woody resprouting species to recruit seedlings after fire in south-eastern Australia and lag years behind species with soil or canopy seed banks. #### **Introduction** In fire-prone habitats, recruitment in plant species is frequently linked to the passage of a fire (Tyler 1995). This results from at least two main mechanisms. First, in species with soil seed banks, seed dormancy may be broken by the passage of fires (e.g. via heat, smoke, charred wood: Keeley 1991; Brown 1993; or interactions of these factors: Keith 1997; Morris 2000). Examples include many legumes (Jeffery *et al.* 1988; Auld and O'Connell 1991) and nonleguminous species (Brown 1993; Dixon *et al.* 1995). Second, in species with canopy seed banks, fires result in the mass opening of fruits and the release of seeds (Bond *et al.* 1984; Lamont *et al.* 1991). However, a number of species have no available seed storage in either the soil or canopy at the time of the passage of a fire (Keith 1996). A few may rely on dispersal from unburnt areas, but most have mechanisms that allow established plants to survive fire via buried lignotubers, rhizomes or buds (protected meristems). These species usually flower soon after fire and then release seeds (Gill 1981; Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Carrington 1999). For species dependant on post-fire flowering for recruitment (pyrogenic flowering resprouters), {2} the timing and magnitude of this flowering will influence opportunities for post-fire seedling establishment. The longer the interval between the passage of a fire and seedling recruitment, the more of the available resources such as light, nutrients and space, are likely to have been captured by other resprouting species or by those species with soil or canopy seed banks that can recruit in the immediate post-fire period. Many individuals of pyrogenic flowering resprouting species in south-eastern Australia appear to have a single post-fire flowering (e.g. *Angophora hispida*, Auld 1986; *Blandfordia nobilis*, Johnson *et al.* 1994; *Lomatia silaifolia*, Denham and Whelan 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Gill and Ingwersen 1976, but see; *X*. *fulva*, Taylor *et al.* 1998). In such cases, this represents the only opportunity for recruitment between fires. For other species, flowering may extend over several years following a fire (e.g. *T*. *speciosissima*, Pyke 1983; Bradstock 1995; Goldingay 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Curtis 1998). However, the timing of recruitment in pyrogenic flowering resprouting species has been little studied and the degree to which each post-fire flowering event contributes to recruitment is unexplored. In the post-fire environment, the impact of seed predation may be reduced due to lower predator abundance and also via predator satiation, in the case of serotinous seed release (Whelan 1995; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). However, the seeds of pyrogenic flowering resprouters are likely to be released after most seeds from serotinous species have germinated and, consequently, would not benefit from any predator satiation effects from serotinous seed release. In addition, populations of predators may have recovered by this time. All pyrogenic flowering resprouters are thought to release seeds in a non-dormant state (Bell *et al.* 1993; Bond and van Wilgen 1996) and hence form transient soil seed banks (*sensu* Parker and Kelly 1989). In this study, we assessed post-fire reproduction and the patterns of seedling recruitment after a wildfire in 1994, in two resprouting species reliant on post-fire flowering for seed production (*Doryanthes excelsa* and *Telopea speciosissima*), from the Sydney area of south-eastern Australia. It is apparently capable of asexual reproduction by branching of the rhizome (Nash 1996). It grows in dry sclerophyll forests and woodlands on soils derived from sandstone containing some clay and is restricted to the Sydney Basin in south-eastern Australia, with three outlying populations in northern New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having apical buds protected in underground leaf bases. It flowers in a large, red inflorescence held up to 5 m above the foliage of the plant (Harden 1990–1993). Fire appears to stimulate flowering, although sporadic flowering does occur in the absence of fire (Nash 1996). The mechanism determining flowering is unknown (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996). *Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br. (waratah—Proteaceae) is a tall shrub, generally 2–4 m, which is also known for its striking red blooms that emerge above the resprouting shrubby vegetation in the post-fire environment. It is common in dry sclerophyll forest and woodlands on the central coast and central and southern tablelands of New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having dormant buds protected in an underground lignotuber (Bradstock 1995). Aerial stems are completely regrown after each fire. #### *Sites* Three sample sites within a 10-km radius were chosen in Royal National Park, about 35 km south of Sydney (34°03′S, 151°03′E). At Site 1, both study species occurred in ironstone woodland vegetation (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Eucalyptus sieberi*, *Corymbia gummifera*, *Banksia serrata*, *Xylomelum pyriforme* and *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*. The shrubby understorey included *Grevillea diffusa*, *Banksia spinulosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa*, *Prostanthera* sp., *Isopogon anemonifolius*, *Acacia myrtifolia*, *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Lomandra* spp. and *Dianella* sp. The vegetation at Site 2 (*D*. *excelsa* only) is Sandstone Gully Forest (D. Keith and M. At Site 3 (*T*. *speciosissima* only) the vegetation is Sandstone Heath (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with a short overstorey of *Corymbia gummifera*, *Eucalyptus obstans*, *E*. *sclerophylla* and *Banksia serrata* and a shrubby understorey that included *Lambertia formosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa* and sedges including *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Restio dimorpha* and *Cyathochaeta diandra*. For *D*. *excelsa*, this represented the only post-fire flowering event, although sporadic flowering in the absence of fire does occur in the species (Nash 1996). A single post-fire flowering event has been observed in several other local taxa that are pyrogenic flowering resprouters (Auld 1986; Denham and Whelan 2000), as well as from elsewhere, although most are herbaceous or geophytes (Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996). In *D*. *excelsa*, following the senescence of the flowering spike, individuals undergo subterranean branching, which may result in asexual reproduction (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996). In *T*. *speciosissima*, there was further flowering in some individuals over the next 4 years after the fire, although no seeds were produced following flowering in 1998 (4.5 years post-fire) or later in our study plots. In *T*. *speciosissima*, there was a trend for the highest seed production in the first two post-fire fruiting seasons, followed by a marked decline in the third. Bradstock (1995) and Pyke (1983) observed a similar trend; however, Pyke (1987) suggested that temporal patterns of flowering may depend on other, unknown factors. Goldingay (2000) presented data indicating that for plants in one population of *T*. *speciosissima*, flowering was prolific for up to 8 years after fire, before declining subsequently. The temporal pattern of post-fire flowering in *T*. *speciosissima* clearly varies with location. Despite flowering only once after the 1994 fire, *D*. *excelsa* was very successful in producing seed, releasing nearly five times as many seeds as *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1 where they co-occurred. Both species took some 2.5 years after the fire to establish seedlings. Other species either cohabiting with *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, or from other fire-prone habitats, established seedlings much sooner. In general, those species with a soil seed bank mostly establish seedlings within the first year after a fire, while those with a canopy seed bank mostly release seed in the first 6 months (Lamont and Barker 1988; Lamont *et al.* 1991) and establish seedlings in the first year (Table 5). Even other species that rely on post-fire flowering for seedling establishment appear to be 0.5–1.5 years quicker than *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* in establishing seedlings post-fire (Table 5). Among other Australian species, Auld (1986) found that for the shrub *Angophora hispida*, establishment occurred within about 18 months, while seedlings of shrubby *Xanthorrhoea* spp. were observed 18 months to 2 years after fire (Benwell 1998; Curtis 1998; Taylor *et al.* 1998). This is also the case in other fire-prone areas of the world, including Californian sage scrub, Florida sand pine scrub and South African fynbos (Table 5). By the time seedlings of *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* are becoming established, much of the space, light and nutrients made available by the fire may have been captured by other species (both resprouting plants and seedlings). This will be particularly the case for seedlings from the second and third fruit crops post-fire in *T*. *speciosissima*. In other vegetation types, resprouting species may be able to continue recruiting new seedlings several years after fire (e.g. *Garberia heterophylla* in Florida, Abrahamson and Abrahamson 1996). Curtis (1998) observed seedlings of the arborescent monocot, *X*. *australis*, at sites unburnt for about 100 years. However, such inter-fire recruitment has rarely been observed in the post-fire environment of *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*. Thus, despite the tolerance of their adults to fire, the persistence of these species may in part be due to their large seed size, which ensures that seedlings have sufficient reserves to establish (Westoby *et al.* 1992; Lamont and Groom 1998), although the relative proportions of different nutrients in these seeds has not been determined (Lamont and Groom 1998; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). Primary seed dispersal for both species produced a high concentration of seeds adjacent to the adult and an exponential decay of seed density with distance. This pattern is typical of a broad range of other plant species (Janzen 1970; Auld 1986; Willson 1992; Hammill *et al.* 1998). However, Hammill *et al.* (1998) found that seeds from species with canopy seed banks were dispersed at considerably greater distances than found here for *D*. *excelsa* or *T*. *speciosissima*. Differences in dispersal distances between our study species and between sites for *T*. *speciosissima* in this study are probably related to the height of the infructescences and the height and density of the surrounding vegetation (Hammill *et al.* 1998). Infructescences of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1 were on average 3.9 m (±0.15 s.e.) tall. For *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 1, infructescences were relatively shorter at 1.85 m (±0.08 s.e.), while *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3 had the shortest infructescences at 0.95 m (±0.08 s.e.). The surrounding vegetation at Site 3 appeared to be denser than at Site 1 and this may have further contributed to the shorter dispersal distances. Dispersal along the ground by wind or water in heavy rains may also have contributed to these dispersal patterns (Harper 1977; Hammill *et al.* 1998). For serotinous species that release seeds shortly after fire, the understorey would be relatively open at the time of seed release, while for *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, considerable post-fire regrowth would have increased the density of the understorey. This may act to limit seed dispersal in *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*. The exclosure experiment indicated that seed losses to mammals and invertebrates occurred in the field (Fig. 2), as has been found for other large-seeded species in similar habitats (e.g. *Banksia* spp., *Isopogon anemonifolius* and *Petrophile pulchella*, Bradstock 1991; *Protea neriifolia*, Botha and Le Maitre 1992; *Grevillea* spp., Auld and Denham 1999, 2001; *Hakea sericea* and *P*. *pulchella*, R. J. Whelan and J. York*,* unpubl. data). Generally, other studies have found greatly reduced predation in burnt sites (Bradstock 1991; Botha and le Maitre 1992), while R. J. Whelan and J. York (unpubl. data) found that survival of seeds among exclusion treatments was extremely variable among fires and sites. The high level of losses observed in this study is more comparable to that found at unburnt sites (e.g. 100% losses, Bradstock 1991; 75–100% Botha and Le Maitre 1992; 82–95%, Auld and Denham 1999), and to that of recently burnt sites for *Grevillea caleyi* (Auld and Denham 2001). Most seed losses were presumably caused by mammals rather than invertebrates, on the basis of the patterns of seed removal and *in situ* damage. Losses were high for clumped seeds, but generally lower for seeds placed singly, implying that local seed density may affect the ability of seed predators to find {11} and subsequently eat seeds. *Andrew J*. *Denham*<sup>A</sup> *and Tony D*. *Auld*

Biodiversity Research Group, NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville, NSW 2220, Australia.

ACorresponding author; email: andrew.denham@npws.nsw.gov.au

*Abstract.* A few resprouting plants in fire-prone environments have no local seed bank (soil or canopy) when a fire occurs. These species rely on post-fire flowering and the production of non-dormant seeds to exploit favourable post-fire establishment and growth conditions. For two such pyrogenic flowering species (*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa and *Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br.), we examined the timing of seed release, patterns of fruit production, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling establishment following a fire in the Sydney region of southeastern Australia. Both species took some 19 months after the fire to flower and the first seeds were released 2 years after the fire. *D*. *excelsa* flowered and fruited only once after the fire. For *T*. *speciosissima*, plants also flowered at least once more in the subsequent 5 years, but produced seed in only the first three post-fire flowering years. Fruit production differed between species, with fruiting individuals of *D*. *excelsa* producing fewer infructescences, similar numbers of follicles, but many more seeds per follicle than fruiting individuals of *T*. *speciosissima*. Ultimately, *D*. *excelsa* produced approximately six times as many seeds per m2 and four times as many seeds per adult in one flowering season than *T*. *speciosissima* did after four flowering (three successful fruiting) seasons.

Seeds were passively dispersed from fruits borne 3–4 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 1–2 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) above the ground. Most seeds were found within 5 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 3 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) of parent plants. The primary seed shadow of both species was a poor predictor of the distribution of seedlings, with more seedlings occurring further from the adults than expected from the distribution of seeds. Seed loss to predators was high in both species in exclusion experiments where mammals had access to clumps of seeds (77–88%). It was variable and generally lower (8–65%) in experiments where seeds were not locally clumped. However, for *T*. *speciosissima*, at one site, some 65% of seeds were lost to mammals and invertebrates in these latter experiments. At this site, these losses appeared to influence subsequent recruitment levels, as very low seedling densities were observed.

For both species, germination of seedlings first occurred some 2.5–3 years after the passage of the fire. The percentage of seeds produced to seedlings successfully established was low in *D*. *excelsa* (2–3%) and more variable across sites and years in *T*. *speciosissima* (0–18%). Resultant post-fire seedling densities of *D*. *excelsa* (two sites) and *T*. *speciosissima* at one site were similar, but they were much lower at the *T*. *speciosissima* site that had high levels of seed predation. Both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* are amongst the slowest woody resprouting species to recruit seedlings after fire in south-eastern Australia and lag years behind species with soil or canopy seed banks.

#### **Introduction**

In fire-prone habitats, recruitment in plant species is frequently linked to the passage of a fire (Tyler 1995). This results from at least two main mechanisms. First, in species with soil seed banks, seed dormancy may be broken by the passage of fires (e.g. via heat, smoke, charred wood: Keeley 1991; Brown 1993; or interactions of these factors: Keith 1997; Morris 2000). Examples include many legumes (Jeffery *et al.* 1988; Auld and O'Connell 1991) and nonleguminous species (Brown 1993; Dixon *et al.* 1995). Second, in species with canopy seed banks, fires result in the mass opening of fruits and the release of seeds (Bond *et al.* 1984; Lamont *et al.* 1991).

However, a number of species have no available seed storage in either the soil or canopy at the time of the passage of a fire (Keith 1996). A few may rely on dispersal from unburnt areas, but most have mechanisms that allow established plants to survive fire via buried lignotubers, rhizomes or buds (protected meristems). These species usually flower soon after fire and then release seeds (Gill 1981; Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Carrington 1999). For species dependant on post-fire flowering for recruitment (pyrogenic flowering resprouters), 

{2}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

the timing and magnitude of this flowering will influence opportunities for post-fire seedling establishment. The longer the interval between the passage of a fire and seedling recruitment, the more of the available resources such as light, nutrients and space, are likely to have been captured by other resprouting species or by those species with soil or canopy seed banks that can recruit in the immediate post-fire period.

Many individuals of pyrogenic flowering resprouting species in south-eastern Australia appear to have a single post-fire flowering (e.g. *Angophora hispida*, Auld 1986; *Blandfordia nobilis*, Johnson *et al.* 1994; *Lomatia silaifolia*, Denham and Whelan 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Gill and Ingwersen 1976, but see; *X*. *fulva*, Taylor *et al.* 1998). In such cases, this represents the only opportunity for recruitment between fires. For other species, flowering may extend over several years following a fire (e.g. *T*. *speciosissima*, Pyke 1983; Bradstock 1995; Goldingay 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Curtis 1998). However, the timing of recruitment in pyrogenic flowering resprouting species has been little studied and the degree to which each post-fire flowering event contributes to recruitment is unexplored.

In the post-fire environment, the impact of seed predation may be reduced due to lower predator abundance and also via predator satiation, in the case of serotinous seed release (Whelan 1995; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). However, the seeds of pyrogenic flowering resprouters are likely to be released after most seeds from serotinous species have germinated and, consequently, would not benefit from any predator satiation effects from serotinous seed release. In addition, populations of predators may have recovered by this time. All pyrogenic flowering resprouters are thought to release seeds in a non-dormant state (Bell *et al.* 1993; Bond and van Wilgen 1996) and hence form transient soil seed banks (*sensu* Parker and Kelly 1989).

In this study, we assessed post-fire reproduction and the patterns of seedling recruitment after a wildfire in 1994, in two resprouting species reliant on post-fire flowering for seed production (*Doryanthes excelsa* and *Telopea speciosissima*), from the Sydney area of south-eastern Australia. We examined (i) the timing of flowering and magnitude of seed production over 5 years after the fire; (ii) the pattern of seed and seedling dispersal; (iii) the level of post-dispersal seed predation; and (iv) the proportion of seeds released that resulted in successful establishment of new plants.

#### **Methods**

#### *Study species*

*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa (Gymea lily—Doryanthaceae) is a large perennial rosette plant with a bulbous rhizome and long broad linear leaves up to 3 m long. It is apparently capable of asexual reproduction by branching of the rhizome (Nash 1996). It grows in dry sclerophyll forests and woodlands on soils derived from sandstone containing some clay and is restricted to the Sydney Basin in south-eastern Australia, with three outlying populations in northern New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having apical buds protected in underground leaf bases. It flowers in a large, red inflorescence held up to 5 m above the foliage of the plant (Harden 1990–1993). Fire appears to stimulate flowering, although sporadic flowering does occur in the absence of fire (Nash 1996). The mechanism determining flowering is unknown (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996).

*Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br. (waratah—Proteaceae) is a tall shrub, generally 2–4 m, which is also known for its striking red blooms that emerge above the resprouting shrubby vegetation in the post-fire environment. It is common in dry sclerophyll forest and woodlands on the central coast and central and southern tablelands of New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having dormant buds protected in an underground lignotuber (Bradstock 1995). Aerial stems are completely regrown after each fire.

#### *Sites*

Three sample sites within a 10-km radius were chosen in Royal National Park, about 35 km south of Sydney (34°03′S, 151°03′E). All sites occurred on soils derived from the Triassic Hawkesbury Sandstone Formation, although Site 1 (with an ironstone influence) and Site 2 (with an alluvial influence) were on soils slightly more fertile than Site 3. At Site 1, both study species occurred in ironstone woodland vegetation (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Eucalyptus sieberi*, *Corymbia gummifera*, *Banksia serrata*, *Xylomelum pyriforme* and *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*. The shrubby understorey included *Grevillea diffusa*, *Banksia spinulosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa*, *Prostanthera* sp., *Isopogon anemonifolius*, *Acacia myrtifolia*, *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Lomandra* spp. and *Dianella* sp. The vegetation at Site 2 (*D*. *excelsa* only) is Sandstone Gully Forest (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Angophora costata*, *Banksia serrata*, *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*, *Eucalyptus piperita* and *E*. *sieberi* and a shrubby understorey that included *Boronia pinnata*, *Grevillea mucronulata*, *Acacia terminalis*, *Lomandra longifolia* and *Caustis flexuosa*. At Site 3 (*T*. *speciosissima* only) the vegetation is Sandstone Heath (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with a short overstorey of *Corymbia gummifera*, *Eucalyptus obstans*, *E*. *sclerophylla* and *Banksia serrata* and a shrubby understorey that included *Lambertia formosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa* and sedges including *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Restio dimorpha* and *Cyathochaeta diandra*. Plant nomenclature follows Harden (1990–1993).

All sites were burnt in January 1994. Before 1994, there was variation in fire history across sites. The eastern part of Site 1 (sampled for *D*. *excelsa*) and Site 3 were burnt in 1988. The western part of Site 1, separated by a road from the eastern part (sampled for both study species), and Site 2 were burnt in the early 1980s (NPWS fire records; D. Keith, pers. comm.).

#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*

The three study sites were monitored to observe flowering after the January 1994 fire for both species up until December 2000. As both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* flower in July–October, this involved seven potential flowering seasons (1994–2000). General observations were also made throughout Royal National Park to determine whether the pattern of the study sites was representative of the general response of the study species to fire in this area. The timing of fruit development and seed release was recorded for the first four flowering seasons after the 1994 fire.

#### *Estimates of seed production and seedling establishment*

Six 30 × 30-m plots were established as follows: *D*. *excelsa*, two plots at each of Sites 1 and 2; *T*. *speciosissima*, one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. For both study species, within each plot at each site, the numbers of infructescences and follicles on all plants were scored each year (1994–2000). *Aust. J. Bot.*, 1983, **31**, 293-6

### **Relationship between Time Since the Last Fire and Flowering in** *Telopea speciosissima* **R. Br. and** *Lambertia formosa* **Sm.**

*Graham H. Pyke*

The Australian Museum, 6-8 College St, Sydney, N.S.W., 2000.

#### *Abstract*

For *Telopea speciosissima* the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all appear to peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter. On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground increases with time since the last fire. For *Lambertia formosa* the density of inflorescences appears to reach a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire.

#### **Introduction**

The effects of fire on the Australian flora are many and are increasingly well studied (see Gill *et al.* 1981). There appears, however, to be little quantitative information on the relationships between time since the last fire and flowering of Australian plants (Gill 1981; Specht 1981). Only for *Xanthorrhoea australis* is there a well established relationship (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971; Gill and Ingwersen 1976; Gill 1981): in some places this species flowers only rarely in the absence of fire (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971).

The aim of this paper is to analyse spatial and temporal variation in flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* (waratah) and *Lambertia formosa* with respect to time since the last fire. This analysis is possible as a result of studies on the pollination biology of these plants and the foraging ecology of honeyeaters that visit them for nectar (Pyke 1980, 1981*a*, 1981*b*).

#### **Methods**

The data presented were collected between December 1979 and December 1981 in the Brisbane Water National Park (lat. 33°32′22″S., long. 151°16′56″E.; elevation 170 m above sea level) and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (lat. 33°36′18″S., long. 151°16′16″E.; elevation 145 m above sea level). In each region, study sites are located in plateau-type, low open-forest (Benson and Fallding 1981) dominated by *Eucalyptus gummifera* (Gaertn.) Hochr., *E. haemastoma* Sm. and *E. oblonga* DC., with a shrub understory composed mainly of *Lambertia formosa* Sm. Both regions are located on plateau tops and hence all study sites have the same aspect. In both regions soils are deep, yellow and earthy (Benson and Fallding 1981) with no apparent differences between the study sites.

The Brisbane Water study site contains two areas in terms of fire history: one area last burnt in December 1976, the other in December 1979. The two areas are separated by a vehicle trail which stopped the more recent fire from spreading further. There are no apparent differences between the two areas in terms of soil or vegetation. The entire Ku-ring-gai Chase study site last burnt in 1965.

Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* has been recorded in two ways. In the 1976 burn study area in Brisbane Water National Park, the total number of flowering plants was recorded for the spring flowering periods of 1979, 1980 and 1981. For each inflorescence

0067-1924/83/030293$02.00


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

294 G. H. Pyke

the total number of flowers, height above the ground and number of fruits were also recorded. In each year peak flowering occurred about mid September with high synchrony among plants. In this area and in the other two study areas, permanent circular plots of 20 m radius were established and the numbers of flowering plants within these circles counted every 3 weeks during spring 1981. The numbers of non-flowering plants in each circle were also recorded for spring 1981. Flowering in *Lambertia formosa* was recorded by counting the number of inflorescences in each circle during spring 1981 and in two of the present Brisbane Water circles during spring 1980. During spring 1981, there were four circles in the Brisbane Water area of the 1976 fire, two in the area of the 1979 fire and two in the Ku-ring-gai Chase area.

#### **Results**

#### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Successive Years*

In the Brisbane Water area which last burnt in December 1976, the total number of flowering *Telopea* plants has declined dramatically since spring 1979 (Table 1). Since spring

**Table 1. Flowering of** ***Telopea speciosissima*** **in areas of 1976 and 1979 fires during successive years**

| Area | Flowering time | Total No. of flowering plants | Mean No. of flowers per inflorescence | Mean inflorescence ht (cm) | Mean No. of fruit per inflorescence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1976 fire | Spring 1979 | 306 | 79·5±0·9 | 162·4±2·5 | 2·45±0·11 |
| | Spring 1980 | 100 | 64·9±1·4 | 186·0±3·4 | 0·86±0·11 |
| | Spring 1981 | 9 | 62·3±3·0 | 228·8±13·3 | 0·56±0·24 |
| | | Sample size | | | |
| 1979 fire | Spring 1981 | 63 | 171·8±4·2 | 138·7±3·1 | 3·74±0·41 |

1979 there have also been decreases in the average number of flowers per inflorescence and in the average number of fruit per inflorescence and increases in the average inflorescence height. The differences between 1979 and 1980 are all significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test); for 1980 and 1981 only the difference in mean inflorescence height is significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test). During spring 1981 in the circles in the 1979 fire area (see Table 1), the inflorescence height averaged less than for any of the flowering periods in the 1976 fire area (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) while the numbers of flowers and fruits per inflorescence averaged more (*P*<0·05, *t*-test).

#### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Different Places*

During spring 1981 the density of flowering plants (i.e. number of flowering plants per circle) and the percentage of plants in flower declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 2). The differences in the percentage of flowering are significant between the 1979 and 1976 (or 1965) burn areas (*P*<0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial) but not between the 1965 and 1976 burn areas (*P*>0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial).

#### *Flowering of* Lambertia

During spring 1981 the peak density of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 3). The differences between the areas are significantly different (*P*<0·05 for comparisons between 1979 and 1976 burn areas and between 1976 and 1965 burn areas, *t*-test).

For two circles in the 1976 burn area, the peak numbers of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined significantly from spring 1980 to spring 1981 (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) (Table 3).


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

Fire and Flowering in *Telopea* and *Lambertia* 295

#### **Discussion**

There appear to be strong relationships between flowering and time since the last fire for both *Telopea* and *Lambertia*. In the case of *Telopea*, the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter (Tables 1 and 2). On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground appears to increase with increases in time since the last fire (Table 1). This undoubtedly reflects the continual growth of the plants, starting from a rhizome, following a fire. The density of *Lambertia* inflorescences reaches a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire (Table 3). No information is currently available on either the cause or the adaptive significance of these relationships.

**Table 2. Flowering of** ***Telopea speciosissima*** **in different areas during spring 1981**

| Area | No. of circles | Mean No. of flowering plants per circle | Mean No. of plants per circle | Percentage of plants in flower |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ku-ring-gai Chase (1965 fire) | 2 | 0·50 | 32·5±5·5 | 1·5 (*n*=65) |
| Brisbane Water (1976 fire) | 4 | 0·75 | 138·8±19·4 | 0·5 (*n*=555) |
| Brisbane Water (1979 fire) | 2 | 23·00 | 105·0±2·0 | 22·0 (*n*=210) |

**Table 3. Flowering of** ***Lambertia formosa*** **in different areas during spring 1980 and 1981**

| Area | Peak No. of inflorescences per circle: 1980 Mean | 1980 s.e. | 1980 *n* | 1981 Mean | 1981 s.e. | 1981 *n* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ku-ring-gai Chase (1965 fire) | — | — | — | 5·5 | 3·5 | 2 |
| Brisbane Water (1976 fire) | 195·5 | 17·5 | 2 | 96·5 | 7·8 | 4 |
| Brisbane Water (1979 fire) | — | — | — | 419·0 | 108·0 | 2 |

This research was supported by a grant from the Australian Research Grants Committee. Permission to carry out research within National Parks was kindly provided by the N.S.W. National Parks and Wildlife Service. Two anonymous referees provided many helpful comments on an earlier version of this paper.

- Garnet, J. R. (1971). 'The Wildflowers of Wilsons Promontory National Park.' (Lothian Publ. Co. and Field Nat. Club: Melbourne.)
- Gill, A. M. (1981). Adaptive responses of Australian vascular plant species to fires. *In* 'Fire and the Australian Biota', eds A. M. Gill, R. H. Groves and I. R. Noble. (Aust. Acad. Sci.: Canberra.)

- Pyke, G. H. (1980). The foraging behaviour of Australian honeyeaters: a review and some comparisons with hummingbirds. *Aust. J. Ecol.* **5**, 343–69.

The differences between the areas are significantly different (*P*<0·05 for comparisons between 1979 and 1976 burn areas and between 1976 and 1965 burn areas, *t*-test).

For two circles in the 1976 burn area, the peak numbers of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined significantly from spring 1980 to spring 1981 (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) (Table 3).


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

Fire and Flowering in *Telopea* and *Lambertia* 295

#### **Discussion**

There appear to be strong relationships between flowering and time since the last fire for both *Telopea* and *Lambertia*. In the case of *Telopea*, the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter (Tables 1 and 2). On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground appears to increase with increases in time since the last fire (Table 1). This undoubtedly reflects the continual growth of the plants, starting from a rhizome, following a fire. The density of *Lambertia* inflorescences reaches a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire (Table 3). No information is currently available on either the cause or the adaptive significance of these relationships.

174:#### *Vegetation Structure and Composition*
176:The classification of the floristic composition of quadrats (10 by 2 m) produced six groups (Fig. 4a) which could be interpreted in relation to topography. Although some groups (I, V) comprised only quadrats from scrub vegetation (Table 1), others (II) were equally distributed between scrub and forest or indicated a distinct preference for one or the other (VI, III). The greatest number of species occurred in forested lower-mid slopes (I), the lowest in wet scrub (IV). Most groups were characterised by gradations of species frequencies although the predominant community in the mid-lower slopes of *Melaleuca-Kunzea-Banksia-Acacia* was distinguished by the high frequency of *Adiantum aethiopicum* in the *Pteridium-Goodenia* field layer. The first two axes of the ordination of the groups (Fig. 4b) accounts for 60% of the quadrat variation. Axis 1 appears to be related loosely to topographic factors such as soil moisture gradients.
