233:#### *Regeneration of* A. verticillata *and Other Species in the Scrub*
235:The development of the ground stratum in response to the exclusion of the larger herbivores from the fenced areas was dramatic (Table 2). The most conspicuous effect in the first 2 years was the increase in cover and height of the scrambling grass, *T. juncea* and the raspwort, *Gonocarpus teucrioides.* Both of these species declined sharply during the drought year of 1982 and only the former recovered its prior vigour (Fig. 10). *P. esculentum* behaved similarly to *T. juncea,* but *G. ovata* declined steadily as its associates increased. The cover repetition of species sensitive to browsing tended to be higher in the fenced plots, although *Coprosma quadrifida* did not conform, due to its development of compact, intricate spiny branches under heavy browsing (Table 2). Species diversity was greater in the fenced plots (26 species) than the unfenced plots (20 species).
239:The density of natural regeneration of the major woody species in the mid-slope area of the scrub in 1982 and 1983 is shown in Table 3. *M. ericifolia* is regenerating vigorously from root suckers and *A. verticillata* is also regenerating well from soil-stored seed. The later species flowered and set seed abundantly in 1984 and thus further replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to have occurred in 1985. The reduction of height and density of *A. verticillata* in the presence of browsing was evident in 1986.
241:The observed germination of soil-stored seed in the field and in seed trays is given in Table 4. The number of seedlings germinating from the seed trays was greatest from the upper 1 cm sample, but the species composition was similar for each depth; therefore, the results were pooled and adjusted to show numbers of germinated seedlings per square metre of soil to a depth of 3 cm. Most species showed greater germination in the trays than in the field, with the exception of *Hydrocotyle hirta* and *V. hederacea.* Some species such as *Bulbine bulbosa, Calystegia marginata* and *Schoenus apogon* appeared in the trays but were not observed in the natural vegetation. The notable absence of *T. juncea,* may be due to heavy grazing preventing normal flowering, since this species is normally present as soil seed in wet forests in central Victoria (Ashwell 1981).
243:The species subject to grazing and browsing are indicated in Table 5. Scat analysis indicates that black-tailed wallabies and the common wombat are the major herbivores and differ in their relative abundance along the topographic gradient. This will affect the proportion of grazing and browsing in different sites. Brushtail possums were present, and may have been responsible for minor browsing of eucalypt seedlings in 1980 within the fenced plots. Hog deer *(Axis porcinus)* are present in the area but do not appear to be as important as the marsupials at this time.

*Aust. J. Bot.*, 1989, **37**, 1-18

# **Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by** *Acacia verticillata* **(L'Hérit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria**

*David H. Ashton and Jennifer A. Chappill*

School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.

#### *Abstract*

Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia.* In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.

### **Introduction**

In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.

The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km<sup>2</sup> and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). #### *Abstract*

Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. In this area the scattered individuals of *A. verticillata* flowered after 5 years, thus restoring to some extent the soil seed bank of this species.

The mid-slope areas show the greatest diversity both structurally and floristically. With the demise of the *A. verticillata* stratum the high percentage of bare ground was subject to the effects of insolation, and regeneration of soil seed commenced. The patchy regeneration of *A. verticillata,* which commenced about 10 years ago, is continuing, but the area available is being diminished as the field layer of *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* increases in area, density and height. Therefore, at this stage, *A. verticillata* has contracted its range to the mid slopes where the previously dense, even-aged stand is being replaced by a patchy, uneven-aged community, with an age span of more than 15 years. Future cycles of regeneration may further exaggerate this tendency and produce a regeneration mosaic, sens. Watt (1947), although severe fires in the next century may again restore an even-aged community from the soil seed bank over the whole topographic range.

Only under very rare instances do eucalypt seedlings survive without the intervention of fire. The experimental plots demonstrate conclusively the overwhelming importance of the herbivore factor in preventing the regeneration of *Eucalyptus* species under otherwise favourable conditions. Much seed is harvested by insects, and seedlings beyond the two-leaf stage are readily browsed. Over the first few years little discrimination occurred between the three contending species in the area - *E. obliqua, E. muelleriana* and *E. baxteri.* When fenced, the latter two species have survived better in the luxuriant ground stratum, possibly as a consequence of their longer period of horizontally disposed juvenile foliage. However, these data may be biased by the different seed sources for *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana* used.

In the event of fire, adequate seed storage in the eucalypt canopy is a prerequisite for regeneration, but even so seed dispersal is likely to be limited to much less than 4-5 tree heights from the source (Ashton 1986). Small areas of scrub, therefore, may be expected to be encroached by eucalypts after fire but this will be a rare event in non-fire periods. Large areas of scrub, therefore, are likely to remain an intractable problem, even if fires of suitable frequency and type occur at times coinciding with abundant eucalypt seed production.

The management of these areas for the ultimate aim of restoration of forest would require the removal or control of the damaging herbivore population, which would be an anathema to the policy of a National Park. The alternative of spot sowing or planting appropriate eucalypt species with fencing guards would provide focal points from which subsequent regeneration may occur under the right conditions of disturbance. However, any measures would be successful only in the long-term because of the magnitude of the area of forest that has been devastated during a century of uncontrolled fire regimes.

In terms of dynamics, the mid and lower slopes represent a relatively stable stage since *A. verticillata* is regenerating; however, much will depend on the growth, toler


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub 17

ance and longevity of other dominants such as *B. marginata,* *C. quadrifida, K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia.* The successfully regenerating species are either unpalatable or spiny at shoot maturity. The importance of the soil seed bank and the ability of species to avoid the sensitive seedling stage by vegetative spread is clearly seen in the potentially dense field and ground strata of this vegetation. In this area the scattered individuals of *A. verticillata* flowered after 5 years, thus restoring to some extent the soil seed bank of this species.

The mid-slope areas show the greatest diversity both structurally and floristically. With the demise of the *A. verticillata* stratum the high percentage of bare ground was subject to the effects of insolation, and regeneration of soil seed commenced. The patchy regeneration of *A. verticillata,* which commenced about 10 years ago, is continuing, but the area available is being diminished as the field layer of *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* increases in area, density and height. Therefore, at this stage, *A. verticillata* has contracted its range to the mid slopes where the previously dense, even-aged stand is being replaced by a patchy, uneven-aged community, with an age span of more than 15 years. Future cycles of regeneration may further exaggerate this tendency and produce a regeneration mosaic, sens. Watt (1947), although severe fires in the next century may again restore an even-aged community from the soil seed bank over the whole topographic range.

Only under very rare instances do eucalypt seedlings survive without the intervention of fire. The experimental plots demonstrate conclusively the overwhelming importance of the herbivore factor in preventing the regeneration of *Eucalyptus* species under otherwise favourable conditions. Much seed is harvested by insects, and seedlings beyond the two-leaf stage are readily browsed. Over the first few years little discrimination occurred between the three contending species in the area - *E. obliqua, E. muelleriana* and *E. baxteri.* When fenced, the latter two species have survived better in the luxuriant ground stratum, possibly as a consequence of their longer period of horizontally disposed juvenile foliage. However, these data may be biased by the different seed sources for *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana* used.

In the event of fire, adequate seed storage in the eucalypt canopy is a prerequisite for regeneration, but even so seed dispersal is likely to be limited to much less than 4-5 tree heights from the source (Ashton 1986). Small areas of scrub, therefore, may be expected to be encroached by eucalypts after fire but this will be a rare event in non-fire periods. Large areas of scrub, therefore, are likely to remain an intractable problem, even if fires of suitable frequency and type occur at times coinciding with abundant eucalypt seed production.

The management of these areas for the ultimate aim of restoration of forest would require the removal or control of the damaging herbivore population, which would be an anathema to the policy of a National Park. The alternative of spot sowing or planting appropriate eucalypt species with fencing guards would provide focal points from which subsequent regeneration may occur under the right conditions of disturbance. However, any measures would be successful only in the long-term because of the magnitude of the area of forest that has been devastated during a century of uncontrolled fire regimes.

37	1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. 57	#### Introduction
58	
59	Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont et al. 1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The
60

72	
73	ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where conditions for seedling recruitment are best immediately following fire (i.e. competition for light, moisture and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the population by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that establish later during the interfire period have a low probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be much younger and, on average, will have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit (*sensu* Stearns 1992).
74	
75	The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant age determines the range of fire frequencies for which population maintenance is possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, then a population is threatened with extinction.
76	
77	In the absence of fire some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the likelihood of plant recruitment and survival to reproductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and plant senescence (Witkowski et al. 1991). This means that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds may survive for many years after the death of parent plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).
78	
79	*Banksia hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia about 250-330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seeds are held in a state of enforced dormancy within woody follicles on large infructescences (cones) in the crown. While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds abort during development, while others are either released gradually or (especially after fire) are consumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).
80	
81	The geographical extent (80 × 30 km) of the low nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the distribution of this species, which is further limited by its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont et al. 1989). This means that the species exists as a large number of discrete populations of varying sizes (< 100 to > 10 000 individuals) separated by distances of 0.2 to > 1 km. The largest populations are located near Mt Adams in the northern part of the species range. Land clearance for agriculture, mining and mineral exploration, and increased incidence of anthropogenic ignition, make habitat loss and increased fire frequency potential threats to the long term survival of this species. In addition, its attractive orange inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed production in exploited populations (Witkowski et al. 1994).
82	
83	This paper describes seed production and availability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana* in relation to plant age (= time since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following questions were posed:
84	
85	1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant age, and what factors influence the rate of seed accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny, granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?
86	
87	2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the optimum fire frequency to which the species is adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible with population survival?
88	
89	#### STUDY AREA
90	
91	The study was located in the Yardanogo Nature Reserve about 330 km north of Perth (29°25′S, 114°58′E). Mean annual rainfall at the two closest climate stations is 513 mm (Eneabba; 55 km to the south) and 471 mm (Dongara; 25 km to the north), respectively. There is a pronounced winter maximum with almost no rain (median 20 mm) in the five summer months from December to April. Temperature regimes are similar for both climate stations: mean maximum temperature in the hottest month (January) is 35.8 °C, mean minimum temperature in the coolest month (July) is 9.2 °C. Soils vary from acidic, leached sands on low dunes to sandy clays in intervening depressions (Hnatiuk & Hopkins 1981). The vegetation of the low dunes is a diverse scrub-heath usually dominated by two *Banksia* species, *Banksia hookeriana* and *Banksia attenuata* R. Br., although up to six banksias may co-occur (Beard 1984; Enright & Lamont 1989).
92	
93	#### Materials and methods
94	
95	Seven sample plots, each 400 m<sup>2</sup> in area and ranging in age since last fire from 1 to 3 and 14-16 years, were established in 1986 and monitored for 6-8 years. They were on the crests and slopes of low, sandy dunes in scrub-heath along the edge of a 2-km section of Mt Adams Road within the Yardanogo Nature Reserve. Sites covering a broader range of *Banksia hookeriana* stand ages could not be located.

The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant age determines the range of fire frequencies for which population maintenance is possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, then a population is threatened with extinction.

In the absence of fire some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the likelihood of plant recruitment and survival to reproductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and plant senescence (Witkowski et al. 1991). This means that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds may survive for many years after the death of parent plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).

*Banksia hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia about 250-330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seeds are held in a state of enforced dormancy within woody follicles on large infructescences (cones) in the crown. While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds abort during development, while others are either released gradually or (especially after fire) are consumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).

The geographical extent (80 × 30 km) of the low nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the distribution of this species, which is further limited by its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont et al. 1989). This means that the species exists as a large number of discrete populations of varying sizes (< 100 to > 10 000 individuals) separated by distances of 0.2 to > 1 km. The largest populations are located near Mt Adams in the northern part of the species range. Land clearance for agriculture, mining and mineral exploration, and increased incidence of anthropogenic ignition, make habitat loss and increased fire frequency potential threats to the long term survival of this species. In addition, its attractive orange inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed production in exploited populations (Witkowski et al. 1994).

This paper describes seed production and availability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana* in relation to plant age (= time since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following questions were posed:

1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant age, and what factors influence the rate of seed accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny, granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?

2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the optimum fire frequency to which the species is adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible with population survival?

#### STUDY AREA

The study was located in the Yardanogo Nature Reserve about 330 km north of Perth (29°25′S, 114°58′E). Mean annual rainfall at the two closest climate stations is 513 mm (Eneabba; 55 km to the south) and 471 mm (Dongara; 25 km to the north), respectively. There is a pronounced winter maximum with almost no rain (median 20 mm) in the five summer months from December to April. Temperature regimes are similar for both climate stations: mean maximum temperature in the hottest month (January) is 35.8 °C, mean minimum temperature in the coolest month (July) is 9.2 °C. Soils vary from acidic, leached sands on low dunes to sandy clays in intervening depressions (Hnatiuk & Hopkins 1981). The vegetation of the low dunes is a diverse scrub-heath usually dominated by two *Banksia* species, *Banksia hookeriana* and *Banksia attenuata* R. Br., although up to six banksias may co-occur (Beard 1984; Enright & Lamont 1989).

#### Materials and methods

Seven sample plots, each 400 m<sup>2</sup> in area and ranging in age since last fire from 1 to 3 and 14-16 years, were established in 1986 and monitored for 6-8 years. They were on the crests and slopes of low, sandy dunes in scrub-heath along the edge of a 2-km section of Mt Adams Road within the Yardanogo Nature Reserve. Sites covering a broader range of *Banksia hookeriana* stand ages could not be located.

Seed production was estimated by counting the total number of cones on a random sample of 10 plants and the number of follicles on each of 10 randomly chosen cones per plant. The onset and level of flower head (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded within five replicate 25-m<sup>2</sup> subplots per plot for each year until 1991 (four plots) or 1993 (one plot).

For the two plots where plant age was 14-16 years in 1986, the total number of plants and total number of cones per plant was determined. For a random sample of 10 plants per plot, the height and crown diameter, and number of new cones was enumerated each year there-after until 1991 (when wildfire killed all plants in one plot) or 1993. Plots were searched each year for evidence of seedling establishment from spontaneous release of seeds in the absence of fire.

Complete cone crops were harvested from 10 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants at the start of the study in 1986. Cones were allocated to annual age classes using the stem node ageing method so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class which had opened in the absence of fire (Cowling & Lamont 1985a). Cones were burned and subjected to wet-dry cycles to induce follicle rupture and facilitate seed removal (Cowling & Lamont 1985b). The numbers of follicles, and proportions of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds were determined per plant by cone age. Viability of firm seeds was assessed by germinating batches of 25 seeds per cone age class from each of five plants (replicates) under moist conditions at 15 °C (Cowling et al. 1987).

#### STATISTICAL ANALYSES

Trends between seed parameters, plant age and cone age were analysed using regression models (SYSTAT 1992). Where data were not normally distributed, logarithmic (ln) and arcsine transformations were employed to satisfy assumptions of the regression models used. All error terms listed are standard errors.

A canopy seed bank dynamics model, written in programming language C++, was used to estimate the pattern of viable seed retention on plants and fate of seeds in relation to age. The model used regression equations and other statistics relating patterns of seed accumulation and loss to increasing plant and cone age. Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') and evenness (V') were calculated for the distribution of viable seed ages by plant age.

A few plants produced inflorescences at 3-4 years of age, but these were all sterile (age 3: mean inflorescences per plant = 0.12 ± 0.06; age 4: mean = 0.92 ± 0.23). Cone production increased until plants were about 15 years old, after which annual production fluctuated widely about an average of 17 cones per year (Fig. 1a; Table 1). Both within and between year variability in cone production per plant increased with plant age.

The total number of cones held in the crown increased continuously with plant age and although the standard error also increased with age, the mean pattern of accumulation showed a consistent trend (Fig. 1b, Table 1).

#### SEROTINY, GRANIVORY, DECAY AND SEED STORAGE
In the absence of fire nearly all follicles remained closed for the first 5 years. Thereafter the rate of spontaneous seed release increased linearly (Fig. 2c, Table 1). After 10-12 years the cones were heavily weathered and many of the seeds decomposed so that few viable seeds remained.
Since plants only began to set viable seed at an age of about 5 years, and little spontaneous follicle rupture occurred in cones less than 5 years old, there was almost no seed loss due to follicle rupture in plants up to 10 years old. Above this age, the percentage seed loss increased markedly: 5% of all follicles on plants were open by age 13 years, 10% by 16 years, and 20% by age 21 years. No seedlings which established in the sample plots as a result of interfire seed release survived for more than one year.
The decline in seed storage with cone age was also attributable to seed loss through granivory and decay (Table 1). Loss of seeds through fungal decay followed a similar pattern to that described for spontaneous seed release due to follicle rupture in the absence of fire. Decay was almost absent until cones were 6 years old, after which the proportion of seeds lost increased rapidly.

Unlike follicle opening and decay, granivory was recorded for all cone ages (Table 1).

By integrating the information on average patterns of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant and cone age, it was possible to model the pattern of storage of viable seeds on an average plant of any age, and to identify the quantities of seeds lost to incomplete seed development, senescence, interfire dispersal (spontaneous follicle opening), granivory and decay. The statistical relationships used in the model have been described above and are listed in Table 1, and a flow diagram of the model is shown in Fig. 3.
The model first estimated the number of new cones produced per year for each plant age up to 25 years using eqn 1 (Table 1). Number of cones per year was set to 17 once plant age reached 15 years (the average for years 15-21). Estimation was stopped at age 25 years since field data were only available for plants up to 21 years. The number of cones was summed for each possible plant age to produce an estimate of the total number of cones held in the crown at any plant age. #### SEED BANK DYNAMICS AND FIRE FREQUENCY
According to Gill (1981) plants are not adapted to fire *per se*, but to a particular fire regime. The number of viable seeds stored in the crown of serotinous plants may largely determine the number offspring left after a fire. The balance between the accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy seed bank as plant age increases, and the loss of viable seeds to spontaneous follicle opening, granivory and decay might appropriately describe the optimum life history strategy for a non sprouting species in relation to fire frequency. The canopy seed bank dynamics model estimates these patterns of accumulation and loss.
Early in the reproductive life of individuals of *Banksia hookeriana* (5-8 years of age) few viable seeds are produced, but few are lost. The absolute number of seeds available for dispersal following fire is small and there is a low likelihood of successful parent replacement given the high rates of seed and seedling mortality typical of the first few years following fire (Enright & Lamont 1989, 1992a,b). Using data on seedling recruitment after fire in Little Desert National Park, Victoria, Gill & McMahon (1986) estimated that parent replacement in *Banksia ornata* populations was unlikely until plants held ≈ 100 viable seeds in the crown. This correlated with a plant age of about 16 years. Independent evidence on recruitment of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams following experimental fires in 1983 and a wildfire in 1984 indicated that between 45 and 90 seeds were released for each re
The total number of viable seeds lost from the canopy during the interfire period increased rapidly with age for plants > 10 years old. Nevertheless, the excess of total viable seeds produced in the plant's lifetime over total losses peaked at age 15 years. As plants continued to age in the absence of fire, total losses approached and finally exceeded the number of viable seeds still in the crown. This was predicted to occur for the average plant by the age of 22 years.
Using the simplifying assumption that self-replace ment, on average, required release of at least 100 viable seeds per parent after fire, an estimate of the finite rate of natural increase (λ) can be calculated for each plant age (= fire frequency) with the maximum value of λ assumed to reflect the optimum strategy (λ as a measure of fitness, sensu Stearns 1992). Populations of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams appear optimally adapted to recurrent fires every 16-17 years (Fig. 5). Fires at this frequency also maximized the number of viable seeds released after fire relative to the total investment of energy and nutrients expended on seed production. Although the size of the canopy seed bank continued to grow until plants were about 25 years old, predicted λ decreased as plant age increased beyond 17 years. Nevertheless, diversity (H') rises only slowly once this optimum is passed and evenness is always high. One possible consequence of dormant seed banks is the presence of seeds produced in different years which might reflect different pollen parents and selective forces (Harper 1977), i.e. it increases genetic diversity of the seed pool. This might help to buffer the species against rapid evolutionary drift, and at the same time increase resilience of the species in the face of fluctuating environmental conditions. The decline in seed storage with cone age was also attributable to seed loss through granivory and decay (Table 1). Loss of seeds through fungal decay followed a similar pattern to that described for spontaneous seed release due to follicle rupture in the absence of fire. Decay was almost absent until cones were 6 years old, after which the proportion of seeds lost increased rapidly.
Granivory within closed follicles by the larvae of two weevils, *Cechides amoenus* (Curculionidae; Cleoninae) and *Eleale aulicodes* (Curculionidae; Cleridae), and a jewel beetle (Bupestridae; *Astraeus* sp.) was observed. Unlike follicle opening and decay, granivory was recorded for all cone ages (Table 1).
#### THE SEED BANK DYNAMICS MODEL
By integrating the information on average patterns of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant and cone age, it was possible to model the pattern of storage of viable seeds on an average plant of any age, and to identify the quantities of seeds lost to incomplete seed development, senescence, interfire dispersal (spontaneous follicle opening), granivory and decay. The statistical relationships used in the model have been described above and are listed in Table 1, and a flow diagram of the model is shown in Fig. 3.
The model first estimated the number of new cones produced per year for each plant age up to 25 years using eqn 1 (Table 1). Number of cones per year was set to 17 once plant age reached 15 years (the average for years 15-21). Estimation was stopped at age 25 years since field data were only available for plants up to 21 years. The number of cones was summed for each possible plant age to produce an estimate of the total number of cones held in the crown at any plant age. The total number of seeds which could be held on the plant, if every follicle on every cone held two seeds, was then determined. Two estimation methods were available and gave almost identical results: one based on mean follicle number per cone for samples

The proportion of seeds lost from cones due to spontaneous follicle rupture in the absence of fire was estimated for each cone age (eqn 3) and multiplied by the estimated number of seeds in that age class. A new total for remaining seeds by plant age was then determined. The total number of seeds remaining was multiplied by the proportion of firm seeds (eqn 4) to eliminate aborted seeds held in closed follicles from future calculations. Predicted total seeds produced per plant by age 25 years was 5800. Plants were likely, on average, to hold 100 viable seeds in closed follicles by the time they were 8 years old, 1000 by the time they were 17 years, and 1400 when they were 25 years (Fig. 4). The annual rate of viable seed accumulation in the crown peaked at 15 years. By the time plants were 25 years old, the combined impacts of follicle rupture in the absence of fire, and decay, resulted in little further net accumulation of viable seed in the plant canopy and more seeds were lost than were gained per year (Fig. 4). The overall canopy seed store represented a declining proportion of the total seeds produced, dropping from about one-half at age 8 years to one-quarter at age 25 years.
Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') of seed ages represented in the canopy seed bank increased continuously with plant age following the onset of reproductive maturity; quickly at first as the number of seed ages represented increased on young plants (H' = 0.66 at 6 years, to H' = 2.00 at 15 years), and then more slowly as the number of seed ages represented on the plant stabilised (H' = 2.28 at 25 years). The continued increase in H' after annual seed production had peaked (15 years) and the number of seed ages represented had stabilised (18 years), resulted from increasing evenness (V') of seed abundance in each age class. Evenness was initially high (V' = 0.95 at 6 years), declined as each year's seed crop increased (V' = 0.80 at 17 years), then increased again as seed production stabilised (V' = 0.88 at 25 years).

#### SEED BANK DYNAMICS AND FIRE FREQUENCY
According to Gill (1981) plants are not adapted to fire *per se*, but to a particular fire regime. The number of viable seeds stored in the crown of serotinous plants may largely determine the number offspring left after a fire. The balance between the accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy seed bank as plant age increases, and the loss of viable seeds to spontaneous follicle opening, granivory and decay might appropriately describe the optimum life history strategy for a non sprouting species in relation to fire frequency. The canopy seed bank dynamics model estimates these patterns of accumulation and loss.
Early in the reproductive life of individuals of *Banksia hookeriana* (5-8 years of age) few viable seeds are produced, but few are lost. The absolute number of seeds available for dispersal following fire is small and there is a low likelihood of successful parent replacement given the high rates of seed and seedling mortality typical of the first few years following fire (Enright & Lamont 1989, 1992a,b). Using data on seedling recruitment after fire in Little Desert National Park, Victoria, Gill & McMahon (1986) estimated that parent replacement in *Banksia ornata* populations was unlikely until plants held ≈ 100 viable seeds in the crown. This correlated with a plant age of about 16 years. The total number of viable seeds lost from the canopy during the interfire period increased rapidly with age for plants > 10 years old. Nevertheless, the excess of total viable seeds produced in the plant's lifetime over total losses peaked at age 15 years. As plants continued to age in the absence of fire, total losses approached and finally exceeded the number of viable seeds still in the crown. This was predicted to occur for the average plant by the age of 22 years.
Using the simplifying assumption that self-replace ment, on average, required release of at least 100 viable seeds per parent after fire, an estimate of the finite rate of natural increase (λ) can be calculated for each plant age (= fire frequency) with the maximum value of λ assumed to reflect the optimum strategy (λ as a measure of fitness, sensu Stearns 1992). Populations of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams appear optimally adapted to recurrent fires every 16-17 years (Fig. 5). Fires at this frequency also maximized the number of viable seeds released after fire relative to the total investment of energy and nutrients expended on seed production. If stands remain unburned for more than 25 years, opportunities for interfire recruitment might increase due to the release of sites within stands resulting from death of old individuals. One possible consequence of dormant seed banks is the presence of seeds produced in different years which might reflect different pollen parents and selective forces (Harper 1977), i.e. it increases genetic diversity of the seed pool. A wildfire in January 1984 burned 117 000 ha of the northern sandplain heath (van der Moezel et al. 1987), an area equivalent to nearly half of the total geographical range of the species. 5:# **Climate drying reduces serotinous seedbanks and threatens persistence in two fire-killed shrubs**
9:#### **ABSTRACT**
15:#### **Introduction**
23:#### [\\***Correspondence to:**
25:#### N. J. Enright
41:{1}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
49:# **Materials and methods**
51:#### **Study species and sites**

97:# **Statistical analysis**
103:### **Results**
105:# *Hakea decurrens*
109:{5}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
111:2017 (Table S2). Stands measured in the 1990s received an average of 8 mm per year (1.2%) less than the 1946–1990 mean annual rainfall during their lifetimes, while stands measured in 2017 received 73 mm per year (11.6%) less [\(Table 1\). Stands measured in the 1990s showed a strong trend of increasing fruit production with age. Reproductive maturity was first evident at 3 years and serotinous fruits accumulated in the plant canopy mostly remained closed until individuals were >20 years old (by 28 years ~20% of fruits had opened and released their seeds in the absence of fire). In contrast, populations measured in 2017 showed very low levels of fruit production at all ages <20 years and higher rates of fruit opening in the absence of fire [\(Table 1\).
113:Across the TSF chronosequence, there was strong evidence of decreased and delayed reproductive output for *H. decurrens* in 2017 compared with the 1990s [\(Table 1, [Figs 2, [3\). Although cones were first present at 3 years TSF for both periods, probability of reproductive maturity was 50% at 3 years and 90% by 14 years TSF in the 1990s but did not reach comparable levels until 15 years and 26 years TSF, respectively, in 2017, representing a 12-year delay [\(Fig. 2*a*, *b*). Estimates of total fruit production in 2017 ranged from 5% to 30% of 1990s estimates for stands of the same age, with differences declining as stand age increased. Modelled total fruit production was seven fruits per plant at 10 years and 20 fruits per plant at 20 years TSF for plants in the 1990s compared with less than one fruit per plant and five fruits per plant, respectively, at the same plant ages in 2017 [\(Fig. 3*a*, *b*).
117:### *Banksia ornata*
121:**Table 1.** Demographic and climate data for *Hakea decurrens* sample populations by time since fire (TSF) and sampling year, Grampians National Park, south-east Australia.
131:{6}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
133:[\(Table 2). Data for *B. ornata* in Little Desert for the 1990s were taken from [Shaw \(1997\) who sampled 250 plants across five TSF sites (50 per site) and compared with data for 439 plants measured in 2017. Stands measured in the 1990s received an average of 8 mm per year (1.8%) less than the 1946–1990 mean annual rainfall during their lifetimes, while stands measured in 2017 received an average of 38 mm per year (8.4%) less.
135:First onset of cone production in Grampians NP was at 5–6 years, and while cone production and accumulation increased rapidly for populations in the 1990s, it was much lower and slower for populations measured in 2017 [\(Table 2\). There was no difference in mean (±s.e.) number of follicles per cone between time-periods in Little Desert NP (13.6 in [Gill and McMahon \(1986\), 12.9 ± 0.6 in [Shaw  [\(1997\), and 14.0 ± 1.1 in 2017). Past studies reported that ~70% of seeds were firm, and ~80% of these viable [\(Gill  [and McMahon 1986; [Shaw 1997). Based on these values, estimated viable seed store per plant in Grampians NP in the 1990s increased rapidly with age following the onset of reproductive maturity, exceeding 100 by age 10 years and 500 by around age 20 years [\(Table 2). A similar pattern of seed accumulation was evident for stands in Little Desert NP [\(Table 2). Maximum seed stores in the 1990s exceeded 1500 seeds per plant in the Grampians and 700 seeds per plant in Little Desert, while [Gill and McMahon \(1986\) found even higher seed stores of around 2000 seeds per plant for stands in Little Desert in the 1980s (Table S3). For stands measured in 2017, seed stores were generally less than half the size at the same age with maximum seed stores of less than 500 per plant [\(Table 2\).
141:{7}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
145:# **Discussion**
151:{8}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
153:## **Time to maturity**
159:**Table 2.** Demographic and climate data for *Banksia ornata* sample populations by time since fire (TSF) and sampling year, Grampians National Park and Little Desert National Park, south-east Australia.
169:{9}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
173:#### **Seed production and storage**
179:{10}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
185:Applying the same principles to *B. ornata*, maximum seed store occurs at age ~40 years and has not changed over time [\(Gill and McMahon 1986; [Morgan *et al.* 2021, [Table 2). However, lower rates of seed production and accumulation will have lowered the potential rate of natural increase and lengthened the optimum fire interval in 2017 relative to the 1990s. These results create the management conundrum that populations require much longer minimum inter-fire intervals and more seeds per plant to ensure that selfreplacement after fire is feasible, but are increasingly likely to have a smaller seed store and experience more rather than less frequent fire. Potentially exacerbating this conundrum
189:{11}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
195:In the present study, low seed availability clearly emerges as a factor that may limit post-fire recruitment for *H. decurrens*, with no measured stands in the northern sector of Grampians NP showing sufficient seed stores for population self-replacement. The 3-year-old stand censused here (burned in 2014, censused in 2017) showed very low plant density, with a large search area (~1 ha) required to obtain the reported sample of 52 individuals ([Table 2). In stands established after fires in the 1990s and earlier, sample sizes of *n* ≥ 50 were readily obtained within plots of 100–400 m2 [\(Enright and Goldblum 1999). In *B. ornata*, current seed stores are around half what they were in the 1980s ([Gill and McMahon 1986\) and 1990s ([Shaw 1997; N. J. Enright, unpubl. data) but may be sufficient for selfreplacement where stands have had at least 20 years since fire to accumulate a seed bank, and drought does not cause post-fire recruitment failure. In our Little Desert site burned in 2015 (24 years at time of fire), 2-year-old seedlings were present at a mean rate of 10 seedlings per pre-fire parent (Table S4). Roughly similar recruitment rates of 14 1-yearold seedlings per parent were estimated from data in [Gill  [and McMahon \(1986\) for a stand of indeterminate age burned in 1977, and of 4–23 1-year-old seedlings per parent by [Shaw \(1997\) for a 13-year-old stand in Grampians NP burned in 1996.

Maximum seed stores in the 1990s exceeded 1500 seeds per plant in the Grampians and 700 seeds per plant in Little Desert, while [Gill and McMahon \(1986\) found even higher seed stores of around 2000 seeds per plant for stands in Little Desert in the 1980s (Table S3). For stands measured in 2017, seed stores were generally less than half the size at the same age with maximum seed stores of less than 500 per plant [\(Table 2\).

#### **Introduction**

[Enright *et al.* (2015) hypothesised potential decline in populations of many woody plant species in fire-prone regions where climate is drying as well as warming, based on the combined impacts of shortened fire intervals, reduced post-fire recruitment and changes to demographic rates during the inter-fire intervals available for plant growth

Most did not address demographic rate change consequences and the authors emphasised the need for more studies on plants (Iler *[et al.* 2021).

# **Materials and methods**

J. Enright, unpubl. data; [Shaw 1997) ([Fig. 1). Summary demographic data were also available from the 1980s for *B. ornata* at sites in Little Desert NP, as reported in [Gill and McMahon \(1986\).

In the absence of fire, plants begin to senesce by age 25–30 years. At stand ages >20 years, some inter-fire establishment may occur as old fruits desiccate and release their seeds following plant or branch death, so that old stands become increasingly multiaged and seed stores decline ([Enright and Goldblum 1999). However, in stands <30 years, inter-fire recruits are readily identifiable as younger and smaller than the original postfire cohort individuals. The raw (individual plant) data for *H. decurrens* reported in [Enright and Goldblum \(1999\) were re-analysed here.

Our protocol was to use rainfall records for the years 1946–1990, starting from the estimated establishment year of the oldest stand censused in this study, as the 'baseline' for comparison with rainfall from 1991 to 2016 (based on our data collection in May 2017). Where there were rainfall data for at least 11 of the 12 calendar months, the missing month was interpolated using the mean rainfall for that month to obtain an estimated annual value. Where there were 2 or more months missing within 1 year, then that year was deemed to be missing and was not used in any analyses. At Halls Gap, the closest climate station to our southern-most Grampians field sites, there were 15 years deemed missing across the available records from 1958 (start of records) to 2016, with nine of these missing in the period after 1990, making it unsuitable for comparison with the baseline 1946–1990 time-period. In addition, a further 5 years used interpolated values. At Dadswells Bridge, the closest climate station to our Grampians field sites overall, the available record was even shorter (1969–2016) and had five missing and nine interpolated years. By contrast, the Nhill climate station (closest to our 
{4}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
Little Desert sites) had almost complete monthly rainfall data from 1946 to 2016, with just one missing and two interpolated years. We ran pairwise correlation analyses for these climate stations across all available years and found highly significant relationships: Nhill vs Dadswells Bridge *r* = 0.852, *n* = 40; Nhill vs Halls Gap *r* = 0.843, *n* = 44; and Dadswells Bridge vs Halls Gap *r* = 0.874, *n* = 27 (*P* < 0.001 in all cases).
To further determine the best source of rainfall data for use in our analyses, we obtained estimated annual rainfall (1960–2016) for the specific latitude–longitude locations of our Little Desert and Grampians field sites from two global climate estimation models, Terraclimate ([Abatzoglou *et al.*  [2018) and ANUclim-WorldClimate [\(Xu and Hutchinson  [2013). Both were highly correlated with each other and with the Nhill, Dadswells Bridge, and Halls Gap climate station annual rainfall data (*r* > 0.90 in all cases). The TerraClimate mean annual rainfall estimates for our sites in Grampians NP for the baseline rainfall period ranged from 595 mm to 630 mm (cf. Dadswells Bridge mean of 580 mm, and Halls Gap mean of 984 mm), and across the full data period to 2016 showed a near-perfect correlation among sites within the Grampians (*r* > 0.999, *n* = 57), as well as between the Grampians and Little Desert (*r* = 0.989, *n* = 57; Fig. S1). Given these strongly correlated patterns in actual and estimated annual rainfall across the whole study region, we used the Nhill climate station annual rainfall data for comparison with *B. ornata* demographic data from Little Desert NP sites, and estimated annual rainfall values using the TerraClimate northern Grampians mean of 630 mm per year and regression relationship to Nhill rainfall for *B. ornata* and *H. decurrens* demographic data for Grampians NP sites (*y* = 1.172*x* + 139.4, where *y* is predicted northern Grampians annual rainfall and *x* is Nhill annual rainfall; *r* = 0.92, *n* = 57, *P* < 0.001; Fig. S2).
To characterise the rainfall history for our censused populations, we determined the rainfall difference from the 1946 to 1990 mean for each *H. decurrens* and *B. ornata*  population based on the span of years for which it was extant. For example, for a stand that was 28 years old when censused in 1995, having established and grown over the post-fire period from 1967 to 1995, growing conditions are expressed as the average deviation from mean 1946–1990 rainfall for each of those 28 years. These data were then used in statistical and descriptive analyses as detailed below.
# **Statistical analysis**
To determine if the reproductive rates for *H. decurrens* and *B. ornata* have changed over time (1990s vs 2017), we fit generalised linear mixed models for the plant-level response variables probability of reproductive maturity and total fruit/cone production for each species in Grampians NP. Statistical analyses were not possible for *B. ornata*  populations from Little Desert NP as we did not have individual-level data for the 1990s, but summary comparisons are reported here based on mean values available from the earlier studies. Probability of reproductive maturity was measured as fruit/cone presence or absence on a live plant. Total fruit/cone production was measured as the total count of open and closed fruits (*H. decurrens*) or cones (*B. ornata*) on a live plant. For each response variable and species combination, we fit two sets of candidate models that considered the effect of stand age (years since last stand-replacing fire) and either: (1) the continuous effect of rainfall change during the plant's life-time (hereafter, rain differential); or (2) the categorical effect of measurement era (1990s vs 2017), representing a broader measure of combined global environmental change impacts that includes warming.
For each species and response variable, we fit models that included the focal predictor (rain differential or measurement era) and stand age, both with and without an interaction term. To compare the magnitude of the effects of predictors, models were fit using standardised predictors (mean-centred per two standard deviations). For each of the eight relationships considered (two species × two response variables × two sets of predictor variables), we evaluated models in the set for outliers, uniform residuals and over-dispersion (count variables only) and selected the model form with an interaction term unless assumptions were violated. Collinearity of predictor variables was assessed prior to model fitting and all models included a random effect of site. Models of probability of reproductive maturity were fit with a binomial error structure while models of total fruit/cone production were fit with a negative binomial error structure. We note that the response variable total fruit/cone is defined differently for each species due to modelling constraints. We modelled *H. decurrens*  total fruits using only individuals with <100 fruits (representing 99.2% of sampled plants) and *B. ornata* total cones using only individuals with at least one cone. We interpreted *P* ≤ 0.01 as strong, *P* ≤ 0.05 as moderate, and *P* ≤ 0.10 as suggestive evidence of effects ([Ramsey and Schafer 2012). Models were fit in *glmmTMB* [\(Brooks *et al.* 2017), diagnostics conducted in *DHARMa* ([Hartig 2021), and effects visualised in *dotwhisker* [\(Solt and Hu 2024\), *ggeffects* [\(Lüdecke  [2018\), *ggplot* [\(Wickham 2016), and *ggpubr* ([Kassambara  [2020\). Analyses were conducted in R version 4.2.2 [\(R Core Team 2022).
### **Results**
# *Hakea decurrens*
We surveyed 842 *H. decurrens* plants in Grampians NP; 444 individuals from six stand ages in the 1990s, and 398 from six stand ages in 2017. There was no evidence of change in plant height in relation to plant age between the 1990s and 
{5}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
2017 (Table S2). Stands measured in the 1990s received an average of 8 mm per year (1.2%) less than the 1946–1990 mean annual rainfall during their lifetimes, while stands measured in 2017 received 73 mm per year (11.6%) less [\(Table 1\). Stands measured in the 1990s showed a strong trend of increasing fruit production with age. Reproductive maturity was first evident at 3 years and serotinous fruits accumulated in the plant canopy mostly remained closed until individuals were >20 years old (by 28 years ~20% of fruits had opened and released their seeds in the absence of fire). In contrast, populations measured in 2017 showed very low levels of fruit production at all ages <20 years and higher rates of fruit opening in the absence of fire [\(Table 1\).
Across the TSF chronosequence, there was strong evidence of decreased and delayed reproductive output for *H. decurrens* in 2017 compared with the 1990s [\(Table 1, [Figs 2, [3\). Although cones were first present at 3 years TSF for both periods, probability of reproductive maturity was 50% at 3 years and 90% by 14 years TSF in the 1990s but did not reach comparable levels until 15 years and 26 years TSF, respectively, in 2017, representing a 12-year delay [\(Fig. 2*a*, *b*). Estimates of total fruit production in 2017 ranged from 5% to 30% of 1990s estimates for stands of the same age, with differences declining as stand age increased. Modelled total fruit production was seven fruits per plant at 10 years and 20 fruits per plant at 20 years TSF for plants in the 1990s compared with less than one fruit per plant and five fruits per plant, respectively, at the same plant ages in 2017 [\(Fig. 3*a*, *b*).

This effect was especially pronounced at younger stand ages; at age 10 years, 9% and 18% decreases from pre-1990s rainfall were associated with 77% and 95% decreases in estimated total seed store per plant. By age 20 years, the same decreases in rainfall were associated with 48% and 73% reductions in estimated seed stores compared with individuals in stands that experienced mean rainfall ([Fig. 3*c*, *d*). 21	(i.e. reduced rates of growth, survival and seed production, and increased time to reproductive maturity). Under their 'interval squeeze' hypothesis, affected plant populations would require longer fire-free periods to reach a demographic state compatible with self-replacement after fire, while climate change impacts on fire regimes and post-fire recruitment conditions would make this increasingly unlikely. A growing body of evidence supports the first two of these interval squeeze drivers as described above, but evidence for shifts in demographic rates directly resulting from climate change remains sparse. [Selwood *et al.*  [\(2015\) reviewed the effects of climate change on species demographic rates based on 147 studies published between 1970 and 2012, finding an overall negative effect of changes in rainfall and temperature on reproduction and survival across a range of fauna (birds, mammals, fish), but noted that there were few published studies for plants. More recently, Iler *et al.* [\(2021\) reviewed the literature on phenology shifts associated with climate change that also had demographic rate consequences, reporting on 238 studies published to 2020. The review showed a continued strong focus on fauna (61% of studies), while of the studies on plants (39% of studies), 77% were experimental, with 73% primarily focused on the effects of shifts in the (typically earlier) onset of flowering. Most did not address demographic rate change consequences and the authors emphasised the need for more studies on plants (Iler *[et al.* 2021).
22	If shifts in key demographic variables are occurring, changes might be seen most clearly in regions with evidence of climate warming and drying over recent decades, such as those with Mediterranean type climates [\(Diffenbaugh and  [Field 2013; [Vicente-Serrano *et al.* 2014). Mediterraneantype ecosystem (MTE) woodlands/shrublands of southern Australia provide an ideal 'field laboratory' for studying this question. These plant communities are woody-fuel dominated and characterised by a crown fire regime with short to intermediate fire return intervals of 10–30 years [\(Keith  *[et al.* 2014; [Enright *et al.* 2015). Short to intermediate longevity (15–50 years) fire-killed shrub and small tree species are prominent and many accumulate a (serotinous) canopy seed store that is readily quantifiable in relation to plant age. This region also shows evidence of ongoing warming since the 1950s and drying over at least the past 30 years [\(Head *et al.* 2014).
23	Here, we capitalise on the rare opportunity to compare estimated seed production and storage for two fire-killed serotinous shrub species of MTE woodlands/shrublands in south-east Australia, *Hakea decurrens* subsp. *physocarpa*  W.R. Barker and *Banksia ornata* (F.Muell.) (both Proteaceae) based on data collected in the 1990s ([Shaw  [1997; [Enright and Goldblum 1999; N. J. Enright, unpubl. data) and again in 2017 in the same or nearby field locations and using the same methods. Our study seeks to provide evidence of a decline in seed production and storage in response to climate change over the past 20–30 years that may threaten species persistence. For both species, we hypothesise that: (1) time to reproductive maturity has increased and fruit/cone production (and estimated seed production and storage) has decreased since the 1990s; and (2) this decline is associated with decreased rainfall under a changing climate.
24	# **Materials and methods**
25	#### **Study species and sites**
26	Data on number of fruits per plant by plant age, seeds per fruit and plant height collected in the 1990s were available for *Hakea decurrens* subsp. *physocarpa* at sites in the northern part of Grampians (Gariwerd) National Park (NP) [\(Enright and Goldblum 1999), and on number of cones per plant by plant age, seeds per cone and plant height collected in the 1990s for *Banksia ornata* at sites in the northern Grampians and in Little Desert NP (N. J. Enright, unpubl. data; [Shaw 1997) ([Fig. 1). Summary demographic data were also available from the 1980s for *B. ornata* at sites in Little Desert NP, as reported in [Gill and McMahon \(1986\).
27	*H. decurrens* is a common understorey shrub that grows to 3.5 m height in open *Eucalyptus baxteri*  (Myrtaceae)*–Callitris rhomboidea* (Cupressaceae) shrubby woodlands on unconsolidated, nutrient-poor sands. Historically, first seed set occurred around 3 years of age, with seeds retained in serotinous woody fruits in the plant canopy for at least 10 years ([Enright and Goldblum 1999). Each fruit contains up to two seeds, and [Enright and  [Goldblum \(1999\) reported an overall seed set and viability of 95.5% (2% aborted, and 97% of the 98% firm seeds viable). Seeds are primarily released as a result of fire and germinate in the first winter after fire (or otherwise perish), establishing single-aged (post-fire recruitment) stands with age equal to time since fire. In the absence of fire, plants begin to senesce by age 25–30 years. At stand ages >20 years, some inter-fire establishment may occur as old fruits desiccate and release their seeds following plant or branch death, so that old stands become increasingly multiaged and seed stores decline ([Enright and Goldblum 1999). However, in stands <30 years, inter-fire recruits are readily identifiable as younger and smaller than the original postfire cohort individuals. Data reported in [Enright and  [Goldblum \(1999\) were collected in 1991 and 1995 and sampled across a time since fire (TSF) chronosequence of stands ranging in age from 3 years to 28 years, representing cohorts established after fires in the period 1967–1992. The raw (individual plant) data for *H. decurrens* reported in [Enright and Goldblum \(1999\) were re-analysed here.
28	*B. ornata* is a prominent species of MTE type shrublands in Little Desert NP, and of open *Eucalyptus*  (Myrtaceae)–*Callitris* (Cupressaceae) woodlands in Grampians NP. It grows to 2.5 m height, and matures at
29	{2}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
30	age 5–6 years, retaining viable seeds in serotinous cones in the plant canopy for at least 30 years [\(Gill and McMahon  [1986). Each cone contains ~13 follicles on average, with up to two viable seeds per follicle [\(Gill and McMahon 1986; [Shaw 1997). Follicles open primarily in response to the heat of fire, and released seeds germinate in the first winter after fire (or otherwise perish), establishing single-aged post-fire stands. [Gill and McMahon \(1986\) found <1% of follicles open on plants up to 50 years old, so that opportunities for inter-fire recruitment are rare. In the absence of fire, plants begin to senesce around age 50 years with most seed likely perishing within rotting cones. Germination rate data from the 1980s and 1990s indicates an average viable seed set of 60% (±s.e. 4–6%) for plants spanning ages 6–50 years and sites spanning both Grampians and Little Desert NP ([Gill and  [McMahon 1986; [Shaw 1997).
31	Individual-level plant data (N. J. Enright, unpubl. data) for a chronosequence of TSF sample populations of *B. ornata*  in the northern Grampians from the 1990s was available for comparison with data collected in 2017. In addition, sitelevel summary data from two previous demographic studies in Little Desert NP were available for comparison with 2017 data. [Gill and McMahon \(1986\) reported data for a TSF chronosequence of sites in and around Little Desert NP (centred on 36.54°S, 141.70°E) spanning stand ages from 1 year to 38 years, representing stands established after fires from 1946 to 1977, and [Shaw \(1997\) for a TSF chronosequence of five stands ranging in age from 4 years to 37 years in the same area.
32	We used total counts of fruits (*H. decurrens*) and cones (*B. ornata*) per plant as a measure of lifetime reproduction. For *B. ornata,* follicle rupture in the absence of fire (i.e. inter-fire seed release) was rarely observed and we used total cone counts to estimate seed production and viable seeds per plant. For *H. decurrens,* open fruits were more commonly encountered, so we recorded both open and

Sample site locations for the Grampians are shown in more detail in the inset (bottom left). Some overlapping sample locations have been separated for clarity. Estimates of viable seeds per plant by species and stand age in 2017 were based on fruit and cone count data from 2017 and germination rate data reported for the earlier time-period by [Enright and  [Goldblum \(1999\) for *H. decurrens*, and by [Gill and  [McMahon \(1986\) and [Shaw \(1997\) for *B. ornata*.
36	#### **Plant surveys**
37	Data for *B. ornata* from the 1990s were collected from a TSF chronosequence of sample populations in the northern sector of Grampians NP, overlapping the burn areas described in [Enright and Goldblum \(1999\) for *H. decurrens*, (fire age data sourced from the Department of Natural Resources and Environment of Victoria, Horsham Office, and our own field observations) ([Fig. 1\). We also included one long-unburned site of unknown TSF that we assigned a notional age of 50 years (so assigned burn year of 1946) based on the large size of individual plants and strong evidence of senescence. TSF maps used for field site selection in 2017 were obtained from the Arthur Rylah Institute, State Government of Victoria (A. Muir, pers. comm.; Little Desert NP fire history maps downloaded on 7 April 2017; Grampians NP fire history maps downloaded on 8 May 2017). Field locations in the same parts of Little Desert NP (*B. ornata* only) and Grampians NP (both species) as used in the earlier studies by [Gill and McMahon \(1986\), [Shaw \(1997\) and [Enright and Goldblum \(1999\) were stratified by TSF and each fire age area was searched for individuals of the target species.
38	We measured plant height and counted total number of open and closed fruits per plant for *H. decurrens* on a minimum of 50 plants at each TSF chronosequence site in Grampians NP (see Supplementary Table S1). We used quadrats of 10 m × 10 m to 30 m × 30 m depending on target plant density and measured all target species individuals within the plots. Plots were placed a random *x*–*y* distance (20–1000 m) from the most readily accessible corner of each mapped burn area and located by GPS. Where plant density was too low to make quadrats a viable method, a random walk to nearest neighbour search approach was used until the minimum sample size was achieved.
39	The same methods were used to collect total cones data for *B. ornata* at both Grampians NP and Little Desert NP (Table S1). For this species, sample size in low density or small burn area sites was sometimes <50. A sample of 30 burned cones was collected (two per plant from 15 plants) from the skeletons of 24-year-old plants killed by fire in 2015 at the Nhill-Harrow Rd West site, Little Desert NP (Table S1) and the number of follicles per cone counted. This assessment was made only on post-fire plants because cones on living plants retain their florets for many years so that follicles are not visible and cannot readily be counted.
40	No viability tests were conducted on seeds for either species in 2017. There were insufficient fruits on individuals of *H. decurrens* to make seed collection feasible (see results below). In *B. ornata,* there was no difference in seed viability in the 1980s vs 1990s based on results reported by [Gill  [and McMahon \(1986\) and [Shaw \(1997\), and follicle set per cone was no different from the 1980s to 2017 inclusive ([Gill  [and McMahon 1986; [Shaw 1997, and data collected for this study in 2017; see results below). Given this, we assume no change in seed viability over the time-period examined in this study. While we acknowledge that seed viability could have changed, such changes are not considered likely to affect the overall conclusions drawn from our study.
41	Other than for wildfires in 1983 and 2014 in the northern Grampians, and 1983 and 2015 in Little Desert, all samples were located in sites last burned by managed (fuel reduction) fires (Table S1). Fire frequency spanning our Grampians study region over the period 1950–2010 is reported by [Coates *et al.* (2010) to correlate with rainfall and fuel accumulation rates, with wetter areas requiring more frequent management burns. They found that most areas in the drier northern Grampians experienced 1–2 fires over this 50-year time-period while those in the wetter south experienced 3–4 fires.
42	#### **Climate data**
43	Monthly rainfall records for Australian Bureau of Meteorology climate stations surrounding our two field regions, ranging from Halls Gap in the south (climate station 079074; 37°14′S, 142°52′E) to Nhill in the north (climate station 078040; 36°31′S, 141°65′E) ([Fig. 1\) were downloaded [\(http://www.bom.gov.au/\)](http://www.bom.gov.au/) and checked for length of record and missing data; i.e. months with no rainfall entry. Our protocol was to use rainfall records for the years 1946–1990, starting from the estimated establishment year of the oldest stand censused in this study, as the 'baseline' for comparison with rainfall from 1991 to 2016 (based on our data collection in May 2017). Where there were rainfall data for at least 11 of the 12 calendar months, the missing month was interpolated using the mean rainfall for that month to obtain an estimated annual value. Where there were 2 or more months missing within 1 year, then that year was deemed to be missing and was not used in any analyses. At Halls Gap, the closest climate station to our southern-most Grampians field sites, there were 15 years deemed missing across the available records from 1958 (start of records) to 2016, with nine of these missing in the period after 1990, making it unsuitable for comparison with the baseline 1946–1990 time-period. In addition, a further 5 years used interpolated values. At Dadswells Bridge, the closest climate station to our Grampians field sites overall, the available record was even shorter (1969–2016) and had five missing and nine interpolated years. By contrast, the Nhill climate station (closest to our 
44	{4}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
45	Little Desert sites) had almost complete monthly rainfall data from 1946 to 2016, with just one missing and two interpolated years. We ran pairwise correlation analyses for these climate stations across all available years and found highly significant relationships: Nhill vs Dadswells Bridge *r* = 0.852, *n* = 40; Nhill vs Halls Gap *r* = 0.843, *n* = 44; and Dadswells Bridge vs Halls Gap *r* = 0.874, *n* = 27 (*P* < 0.001 in all cases).
46	To further determine the best source of rainfall data for use in our analyses, we obtained estimated annual rainfall (1960–2016) for the specific latitude–longitude locations of our Little Desert and Grampians field sites from two global climate estimation models, Terraclimate ([Abatzoglou *et al.*  [2018) and ANUclim-WorldClimate [\(Xu and Hutchinson  [2013). Both were highly correlated with each other and with the Nhill, Dadswells Bridge, and Halls Gap climate station annual rainfall data (*r* > 0.90 in all cases). The TerraClimate mean annual rainfall estimates for our sites in Grampians NP for the baseline rainfall period ranged from 595 mm to 630 mm (cf. Dadswells Bridge mean of 580 mm, and Halls Gap mean of 984 mm), and across the full data period to 2016 showed a near-perfect correlation among sites within the Grampians (*r* > 0.999, *n* = 57), as well as between the Grampians and Little Desert (*r* = 0.989, *n* = 57; Fig. S1). Given these strongly correlated patterns in actual and estimated annual rainfall across the whole study region, we used the Nhill climate station annual rainfall data for comparison with *B. ornata* demographic data from Little Desert NP sites, and estimated annual rainfall values using the TerraClimate northern Grampians mean of 630 mm per year and regression relationship to Nhill rainfall for *B. ornata* and *H. decurrens* demographic data for Grampians NP sites (*y* = 1.172*x* + 139.4, where *y* is predicted northern Grampians annual rainfall and *x* is Nhill annual rainfall; *r* = 0.92, *n* = 57, *P* < 0.001; Fig. S2).
47	To characterise the rainfall history for our censused populations, we determined the rainfall difference from the 1946 to 1990 mean for each *H. decurrens* and *B. ornata*  population based on the span of years for which it was extant. For example, for a stand that was 28 years old when censused in 1995, having established and grown over the post-fire period from 1967 to 1995, growing conditions are expressed as the average deviation from mean 1946–1990 rainfall for each of those 28 years. These data were then used in statistical and descriptive analyses as detailed below.
48	# **Statistical analysis**
49	To determine if the reproductive rates for *H. decurrens* and *B. ornata* have changed over time (1990s vs 2017), we fit generalised linear mixed models for the plant-level response variables probability of reproductive maturity and total fruit/cone production for each species in Grampians NP. Statistical analyses were not possible for *B. ornata*  populations from Little Desert NP as we did not have individual-level data for the 1990s, but summary comparisons are reported here based on mean values available from the earlier studies. Probability of reproductive maturity was measured as fruit/cone presence or absence on a live plant. Total fruit/cone production was measured as the total count of open and closed fruits (*H. decurrens*) or cones (*B. ornata*) on a live plant. For each response variable and species combination, we fit two sets of candidate models that considered the effect of stand age (years since last stand-replacing fire) and either: (1) the continuous effect of rainfall change during the plant's life-time (hereafter, rain differential); or (2) the categorical effect of measurement era (1990s vs 2017), representing a broader measure of combined global environmental change impacts that includes warming.
50	For each species and response variable, we fit models that included the focal predictor (rain differential or measurement era) and stand age, both with and without an interaction term. To compare the magnitude of the effects of predictors, models were fit using standardised predictors (mean-centred per two standard deviations). For each of the eight relationships considered (two species × two response variables × two sets of predictor variables), we evaluated models in the set for outliers, uniform residuals and over-dispersion (count variables only) and selected the model form with an interaction term unless assumptions were violated. Collinearity of predictor variables was assessed prior to model fitting and all models included a random effect of site. Models of probability of reproductive maturity were fit with a binomial error structure while models of total fruit/cone production were fit with a negative binomial error structure. We note that the response variable total fruit/cone is defined differently for each species due to modelling constraints. We modelled *H. decurrens*  total fruits using only individuals with <100 fruits (representing 99.2% of sampled plants) and *B. ornata* total cones using only individuals with at least one cone. We interpreted *P* ≤ 0.01 as strong, *P* ≤ 0.05 as moderate, and *P* ≤ 0.10 as suggestive evidence of effects ([Ramsey and Schafer 2012). Models were fit in *glmmTMB* [\(Brooks *et al.* 2017), diagnostics conducted in *DHARMa* ([Hartig 2021), and effects visualised in *dotwhisker* [\(Solt and Hu 2024\), *ggeffects* [\(Lüdecke  [2018\), *ggplot* [\(Wickham 2016), and *ggpubr* ([Kassambara  [2020\). Analyses were conducted in R version 4.2.2 [\(R Core Team 2022).
51	### **Results**

71	# **Discussion**
72	Reported climate change impacts on the demographic rates of plant species of fire-prone ecosystems, and their potential population dynamic consequences, are rare relative to impacts relating to fire regimes [\(Jones *et al.* 2022) and post-fire recruitment [\(Davis *et al.* 2019). We investigated the hypothesis that there would be decreases in rates of seed production and storage due to climate drying for populations of two fire-killed shrub species from MTE woodlands/ shrublands in south-east Australia. We found markedly slowed time to reproductive maturity and reduced levels of seed production and storage at comparable plant ages for populations of both species measured in 2017 compared with the 1990s and related to decreased rainfall. The consistent significance of time period of study (1990s vs 2017; referred to as 'Era' in our results) also suggests a role for increasing temperature (most likely exacerbating water stress) in our findings. These results are similar to those reported for *B. hookeriana* in MTE shrublands in southwest Australia where rainfall has declined by ~20% since the mid-1970s (Keith *[et al.* 2014; [Enright *et al.* 2015), providing strong evidence of a demographic shift that, in combination with increasing fire activity, may threaten persistence of some species.
